# MQ-C05-015 — Seventh investigation: disputed additional attributes, persistence, formation, and scriptural predicates

**Arabic source:** source characters 1160086–1171039 (exclusive), printed volume II pp.105–110. **Status:** source-ordered first-pass explanatory translation; technical attribution and printed readings unverified.

### Are there attributes in addition to the seven affirmed before?

The subject is attributes **disputed even among the people of truth who affirm beginningless divine attributes**. Some literalists maintain that no attribute exists beyond the seven previously mentioned. They offer two grounds. **First**, no proof establishes any further attribute, and what has no proof must be denied. Both premises are denied. Absence of a known demonstration is not demonstration of absence. **Second**, we are commanded to attain perfect knowledge of God, including His essence and all His attributes. Were there additional attributes, the perfected knowers among us would necessarily know them, whereas it is manifest that they do not. They add that attributes can be known only from God's acts and from denial of deficiencies, and neither method establishes anything further. The answer is that religious responsibility is **according to one's capacity**, not an unlimited comprehensive grasp; even accepting the premise, the opponent has not shown that perfected knowers lack all knowledge of further attributes. Nor are the suggested means the only path to knowledge: **revelation** is also a reliable source.

### The attribute of persistence (*baqāʾ*)

Among the disputed attributes is **persistence**. Al-Ashʿarī and some Sunni followers affirm an additional eternal attribute called *baqāʾ*: the Necessary Existent is certainly abiding, and, they reason, an abiding subject must possess an underlying positive reality through which it abides, just as a knower possesses knowledge and a powerful one power. Persistence is neither a mere negation nor relation, they say, and cannot be reduced to existence, since a thing may exist and then cease—especially transient accidents.

Most theologians deny that persistence is a **positive attribute additional to existence**. Four arguments are reviewed.

**First**, what persistence signifies is simply the **continuance of existence**. To say that a thing exists at a second time after existing at a first is not to identify a second real accident over and above its existence; it is to regard that existence under a temporal comparison.

**Second**, were the Necessary Existent to abide through a persistence other than His essence, He would not be **necessary through Himself**. What exists necessarily through its essence also remains through its essence; what belongs essentially cannot depart. On an account defining *baqāʾ* as the property by which a subject exists at the second time, the difficulty is even clearer: God's existence at that time would depend upon a reality other than Himself. The author of *al-Ṣaḥāʾif* objects that the only dependence need concern one attribute's dependence on another attribute deriving from the essence, as willing depends on knowledge and knowledge on life. But existence itself is not an attribute inhering in a substrate in precisely that way; even granting such language, dependence of the Necessary's existence on something apart from His essence conflicts with the thesis of necessity through essence.

**Third**, suppose the essence persists by an additional persistence. If that persistence must itself depend on the essence, the existence of each in the later time seems to depend on the other, giving a circle. If, conversely, the essence depends on persistence while persistence is self-sufficient, one has made **persistence rather than the essence** the truly necessary thing. The author of *al-Mawāqif* suggests that both could exist simultaneously without either depending upon the other. But that grants two self-sufficient necessary beings, and in any case the independence of a **divine attribute** from the divine essence contradicts the very notion of an attribute.

**Fourth**, an additional eternal attribute of persistence would itself have to **persist**. If through a second persistence, the problem repeats indefinitely, besides introducing the contested inherence of an accident in another accident (*qiyām al-maʿnā bi-l-maʿnā*). If through itself, why may God not likewise persist **by Himself**, without the additional property? The affirmers reply that persistence's persisting through itself is no more problematic than existence's existing through itself or eternity's being eternal through itself. But the problem persists in a sharpened form: eternal **knowledge and power** must also abide. If their *baqāʾ* is different from them, does one need countless additional persisting eternal attributes, and must these accidents inhere in other accidents? If each attribute abides by itself, why require a distinct abiding property for the essence? Several attempted answers follow.

**First answer**, attributed to some ancients: say that the divine essence persists **with its attributes**, not that the attributes themselves persist. This is unacceptable, for the persistence of an eternal attribute is itself evident.

**Second answer**, attributed to some Ashʿarites and reportedly to al-Ashʿarī, holds that **knowledge persists by a persistence identical with knowledge**, and likewise with the other attributes. That is, one and the same knowledge makes the essence knowing and makes that particular knowledge itself abiding, without making the knowledge *knowing of itself*. The persistence of the essence is a separate attribute of persistence, and each attribute can be identical with its own continuing persistence without becoming another knowledge or power. The analogy is a body which is in a region through a mode of being-located distinct from itself; the mode of being-located need not itself have a second mode of being-located in order to be present. One must distinguish the **subject** to which a predicate applies and the **capacity** under which it applies. That a thing's persistence is identical with itself does not make that thing a knowing or powerful substance.

Yet the same difficulty returns: if knowledge can persist by its own reality, why cannot the **divine essence** persist by its own essence? To assert that added attributes are the normal rule except when a vicious inherence results is no demonstration; it can be opposed by the maxim that unnecessary proliferation of eternal realities should be excluded without decisive proof.

**Third answer**, attributed to al-Ashʿarī, holds that the attributes persist through the **very persistence by which the essence persists**, because they are not wholly other than the essence, unlike a created substance and its accidents. One may object that the attributes are not identical with the essence either; an attribute's persistence cannot simply be an accident inhering in something **neither identical with nor fully other than** its own subject without explanation. A further objection says that, if a common persistence makes the attributes abiding, a common knowledge should make them knowing and a common power powerful. The reply distinguishes that knowledge is not an appropriately predicable attribute of **another attribute**, whereas *abiding* does truly apply to knowledge. That answer protects the particular case but does not remove every metaphysical question about the underlying account.

### The Māturīdī attribute of formation (*takwīn*)

Another disputed attribute is **formation or bringing-into-being** (*takwīn*), famously affirmed by Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī and his followers. They attribute the doctrine to theologians before Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī and interpret the saying of Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭaḥāwī, “He has lordship without anyone over whom He is lord, and creatorship without any creature,” as pointing toward it. They define *takwīn* as **bringing a nonexistent from nonexistence into existence**. They argue extensively that it is beginningless, different from **power** (*qudra*), and other than the **thing formed** (*mukawwan*), while its eternity does not make the produced things eternal. The author remarks, however, that they have not sufficiently answered the principal question: **why must this attribute differ from power when power is taken as related to one of the two alternatives of acting or not acting and conjoined with will?**

Their principal positive argument is that God unquestionably **forms and brings about** things, and to do so without a property through which He is a former would be as unintelligible as a knower without knowledge. This property must be eternal, for an originated property cannot inhere in the divine essence. Its names vary with its objects: in producing creatures it is **creating** (*takhlīq*); in providing livelihood, **provisioning** (*tarzīq*); in giving configurations, **forming** (*taṣwīr*); in giving life, **enlivening** (*iḥyāʾ*); in causing death, **putting to death** (*imāta*), and similarly for the rest.

**Reply:** the analogy applies to **genuine positive attributes** such as knowledge and power. The actual production of an effect need not be another real inhering attribute; it can be a relation conceived between **producer and product**. Such a relation arises with the product and does not have independent eternal external existence. **Power and will** provide what is required for the production of the effect.

Three further Māturīdī arguments are reported. **(1)** In eternal speech God praises Himself as Creator, Originator and Fashioner. If actual creating and fashioning begin only later, this would praise Him for something not then present and would mean that an additional perfection came to belong to Him after previously being absent. **Reply:** revelation also says that those in the heavens and earth **glorify** Him, and that He is God **in heaven and on earth**, with the latter understood in relation to being worshipped. Such attributions can concern what exists at appropriate times, not independently present creatures from eternity. Speaking of future heaven, earth and prophets in eternal divine knowledge or speech does not put those creatures into eternal existence. God is eternally such that the required relationships and effects will obtain when their times arrive.

**(2)** Ashʿarites read the scriptural “Our saying to a thing, when We will it, is only to say ‘Be!’ and it is” as teaching that God's customary production of things occurs at their proper times through the **eternal word 'Be!'**. The Māturīdī asks whether this is not essentially the *takwīn* which he affirms. **Reply:** if the doctrine is simply about an eternal word, it returns to **speech**, not another distinct attribute; and most readers treat the passage as a figure for the speed and certainty of production by perfect knowledge, power and will.

**(3)** Formation is a **perfection**; absence of formation in eternity would therefore have made God deficient. **Reply:** the argument works only if the proposed perfection can literally obtain in eternity as an actual produced effect. God's eternal **power to create** is undisputed; what is questioned is whether there exists an additional eternal external activity of creating before any creature exists.

### Two arguments against additional eternal *takwīn*

**First**, *takwīn* as its adherents defined it is **actual causing to exist**, the bringing of nonexistence into existence. This expresses a relation between an influence and its product, not something separately present as an additional external thing in eternity. **Second**, an eternal actual **producing** seems to require an eternal **produced thing**, because an effect cannot be actually produced without an effect.

The Māturīdī answer distinguishes a beginningless attribute **by which** creatures are brought about *when their times occur* from power considered alone. Power makes each alternative **possible**; *takwīn* makes the effect **actual at its proper time**. Even if *takwīn* is understood as a continuous act of bringing-into-being, its lasting eternally until the created object occurs does not mean it has been an inefficacious transitory blow without anything struck; the critic's analogy with striking without something struck applies only to an accident of action which ceases immediately.

The present author's central demand is repeated: **what proves that such a property is different from power conjoined with willing one determinate alternative?** The authors of the *takwīn* account define power as an attribute that effects what accords with will. Taken by itself, power does not necessitate any particular effect; when joined to a willing determination, the determinate effect follows. This already appears to provide the desired explanation. Al-Rāzī formulates a dilemma. Taken in itself, the proposed *takwīn* either produces by way of **possibility**, in which case it is not distinguished from power, or by way of **necessity**, in which case the Necessary acts by intrinsic compulsion rather than choice. An objection says necessary production *following a voluntary choice* does not remove freedom. The answer is that this necessary sequence after willing belongs to the first branch: it is not a necessity of the proposed attribute **in itself**.

### “Formation is the formed thing,” and other putative attributes

It is commonly reported that al-Ashʿarī identifies **the act of producing** with **the thing produced** (*al-takwīn ʿayn al-mukawwan*). Read literally, this is untenable. One explanation makes the word *creation* a familiar name for creatures, whether by primary usage or common extension, but that is too merely lexical for the metaphysical question. A more promising interpretation distinguishes what **actually occurs externally** when an agent brings about an effect—the effect itself—from the agent's *causing it to be*, which is a **rationally considered relation**, not an independently existing additional external entity. This recalls the discussion of general matters.

Other suggestions are reviewed briefly. Ibn Saʿīd posits **beginninglessness** (*qidam*) as an added attribute making God beginningless, and mercy, generosity and satisfaction as attributes other than will, without adequate demonstration. The Qāḍī adds perceptions of **smell, taste and touch** over and above knowledge; the evidence for additional distinct divine faculties is not established here.

### Expressions of revelation that cannot be understood corporeally

Some scriptural descriptions—**establishing upon the Throne** (*istiwāʾ*), God's **hand**, **face**, and **eye**—cannot be taken in a literal physical sense without anthropomorphism. One report from al-Ashʿarī makes each designate an attribute additional to the seven. The majority, and another opinion attributed to al-Ashʿarī, understand them as **figurative or representational expressions**. Being established upon the Throne indicates sovereignty or a vivid depiction of divine majesty; **hand** indicates power; **face** indicates existence or essence; **eye** indicates seeing or protective oversight.

**Objection:** if all created things are formed by the same divine power, why is Adam specially said to have been created “with My two hands”? Why the dual **two**? Similarly, why the plural “with Our eyes”? **Reply:** expressions of perfected power and special attribution honor Adam; the ship's sailing “under Our eyes” means that it sails within divine care, protection and preservation, just as someone described as being “within the king's sight and hearing” is one whom the ruler watches and protects. Reading “eyes” as the springs that burst forth from the earth has been proposed but is remote in this context.

The author closes with an important explanation from investigators of **rhetoric** (*balāgha*). Reducing *istiwāʾ* to lordship, *hand* and *right hand* to power, and *eye* to perception helps immediately repel the suspicion of bodily likeness. At a deeper rhetorical level, however, the expressions are **representations**, giving sensory form to meanings that are intelligible rather than bodily. They do not simply substitute one isolated dictionary term for another. He points to his own commentary on *al-Talkhīṣ* for the fuller rhetorical treatment.

*Editorial note:* The text does **not** establish that Māturīdīs deny divine power or that Ashʿarites deny any real act of creation. The dispute is whether *takwīn* is an additional beginningless attribute **distinct from power and will**, and what precisely it means for an act and its product to be different.

# MQ-C05-016 — Fourth chapter, first investigation: the possibility and occurrence of seeing God (*ruʾyat Allāh*)

**Arabic source:** source characters 1171039–1203042 (exclusive), printed volume II pp.110–122. **Status:** detailed explanatory first-pass translation, source order retained; not individually checked against printed page images or every Arabic clause.

### The precise point of disagreement

The fourth chapter concerns two matters: whether God may be **seen**, and whether His reality can be known in its essence. Sunni theologians hold that **vision of God is possible** and that believers **will see Him in Paradise**, without confrontation (*muqābala*), spatial direction (*jiha*), or place (*makān*). Other schools oppose them in different ways; the anthropomorphists and Karrāmiyya, as represented here, affirm vision **in direction and place**, since they assign body to God, and thus do not affirm the kind of nonspatial vision at issue. The disagreement is not about the possibility of complete **intellectual disclosure or knowledge**, which the opponents admit, nor about an image being impressed upon the eye or a ray from it contacting the object, which our school admits cannot occur with God.

The disputed state must therefore be distinguished with care. To know the sun from a description or definition is one cognition; to have seen it and then close one's eyes leaves another degree of familiarity; opening one's eyes provides an immediate perceptual condition beyond the earlier two, which is called **vision**. In this life it ordinarily belongs to objects in a direction and place. The question is whether **that kind of perceptual apprehension** can occur without spatial confrontation and relate to the divine essence, which has no direction or place. Advocates of vision use not merely scriptural proofs that it **will** occur, which would imply possibility, but preliminary arguments that it **can** occur; the opponent may reject a scriptural interpretation precisely by denying such possibility. A legal presumption that a thing is possible unless proved impossible may help in private inquiry, but in formal disputation a positive argument is called for. Some of these arguments nevertheless depend on transmitted facts; the claims that Moses requested vision and that the request was tied to the mountain's standing are scriptural premises accepted as certain even by the opponent.

### First argument from Moses' request

God reports Moses asking: **“My Lord, show me, that I may look at You”** (*rabbi arinī anẓur ilayka*). If the divine essence could not possibly be seen, Moses would not have requested to see it. He certainly made this request according to the Qurʾānic text, communal agreement and accepted transmission. A prophet intimate in conversation with God must either have known what can and cannot be predicated of God—in which case requesting a self-evident impossibility would be vain and inappropriate—or not have known it, in which case his standing as a prophetic interlocutor would be called into question.

The Muʿtazilites propose several answers. **(1)** Moses sought not vision but its alleged consequence, **necessary knowledge**. **(2)** An object is understood as omitted: “Show me **a sign** of Yours, so that I may look at Your sign.” The response is that neither reading is required by the words and neither agrees with God's reply, **“You will not see Me”**: that denies seeing God Himself, not acquiring necessary knowledge or seeing a sign. Moses already knew his Lord, heard His words, received extraordinary signs, and spoke to Him; why should he frame ordinary necessary knowledge as though it were a new request? The mountain's being shattered is itself a great sign, whereas the relevant condition is that it **remain standing**, not be destroyed. The construction “look **to** You,” with *ilā*, is taken in the *Irshād* as particularly explicit for looking with vision. A formulation attributed to *al-Mawāqif* that “seeing” when construed with *ilā* scarcely means knowledge is imprecise, since in the verse it is **looking** (*naẓar*) which is joined to *ilā*, not the verb *raʾā*.

**(3)** Al-Jāḥiẓ and followers say that Moses asked **for the sake of his people** when they demanded “Show us God openly.” He attributed the request to himself so that its rejection would make the impossibility clearer for them. The reply protests that Moses did not ask “Show **them** so that **they** may look.” If the request were religiously impossible or even unbelief, as many Muʿtazilites maintain, a prophet should not let its apparent permissibility stand uncorrected. When his people asked for another god, Moses immediately rebuked their ignorance. Nor does the answer explicitly establish **impossibility**, but at most a denial of this particular occurrence. Further, those punished for audacious demands might have been punished for obstinate testing of Moses, not for the mere request of a proposition intrinsically impossible.

Different reconciliations are attributed to Muʿtazilites: that those requesting it already believed but did not know the ruling on vision; that they were neither firmly believing nor openly unbelieving; or that they needed to hear the reply from God rather than Moses and the request was put into Moses' own mouth to remove a supposed excuse. The author objects that the persons who said “We shall not believe you until we see God openly” were not necessarily the **seventy present at Moses' later request**. Those present as recognized followers should have accepted Moses' instruction. If those absent refused to believe a prophet sustained by miracles, they would scarcely be persuaded by the unsupported testimony of seventy representatives. These replies blur historical circumstances rather than settling the argument.

**(4)** Moses knowingly asked an impossibility to obtain additional assurance by joining scriptural testimony to rational proof, as Abraham requested to be shown how the dead are raised. The reply distinguishes a search for confirmation from **deliberately requesting what cannot occur** in words naturally implying uncertainty about God. **(5)** It is suggested that a person may know God without considering every separate question about seeing Him: Moses could have been occupied by other sciences and duties, and asked to learn a point he had not investigated; he then repented for having failed to investigate in advance, or had already begun investigating and sought direct settlement. The author's response is severe: such an explanation assigns God's prophet ignorance about what is possible for God and makes him less knowledgeable than ordinary disputants. The first argument can be arranged in formal disputation as successive denials—that Moses requested actual vision, that a sincere request would otherwise imply ignorance or vain activity, or that ignorance of the issue is impossible for him. Answers must meet the particular premise contested.

### Second argument: vision was attached to a possible condition

God made Moses' seeing Him conditional upon the **mountain remaining stable**. The mountain's stability is intrinsically possible. What is conditionally promised upon a possibility must itself be possible: conditional occurrence means that **under the hypothesis of the condition**, the conditioned occurrence follows, whereas the impossible cannot occur under any hypothesis of a possible condition.

**Objection:** the mountain was required to stand **after** divine manifestation, at precisely the time it shuddered and was crushed. Its stability then was impossible. **Reply:** the **intrinsic** possibility of stability is not destroyed because the mountain actually moved. It is impossible for motion and rest to be present together, but the mountain's **being at rest instead of moving** is possible. The very description that God *made it crumble* presupposes that it could have been otherwise. The analogous possibility of a seated person standing concerns standing **instead of** sitting, not standing and sitting simultaneously. The opponent distinguishes intrinsic possibility from future possibility; the reply denies that a real intrinsic possibility has been shown to vanish merely because one of two alternatives actually obtains.

A further version regards the conditional as concerning *the mountain's stability as such*, without any timing restriction. The objector observes that the mountain was stable at some time, which would imply that vision had occurred. The reply restores the contextual restriction: stability **at the future occasion following the manifestation**, indicated by the particle *fa*, not just stability at any time. Another objection states that a condition's occurrence does not necessitate the occurrence of what depends on it. That is true when *condition* means a merely **necessary prerequisite** of a result. Here it is a **conditional antecedent** to which the occurrence is suspended in the utterance, conceived as completing all that is requisite for the consequent. Other objections say that the verse aims only to show vision's **nonoccurrence**, not its possibility, or aims to extinguish hope rather than to encourage it. The author replies that the inference to possibility holds even when possibility is not the express aim, and that the wording is not unambiguously discouraging. The claim that since the mountain did not stand vision is forever impossible is plainly invalid.

Two less persuasive considerations are mentioned: God replied “You **will not see Me**,” not “I am not capable of being seen,” as might be appropriate if Moses' request were intrinsically impossible; and the report, attributed by Ibn Fūrak to al-Ashʿarī, that God's self-disclosure to the mountain meant He created in it life and sight, so that it perceived Him. The author does not regard these as strong proofs.

### Third argument: existence as the common ground of visibility

Earlier Sunni theologians reasoned that we see **substances and accidents**—bodies, lights, colours and states of being-located. If being susceptible of vision has a common ground in two fundamentally different categories, that ground cannot be what is special to substance or accident. It must be something shared; the proposed candidates are **existence** and **origination**. Origination is a rationally considered fact, either the precedence of nonexistence or existence following nonexistence, and its nonexistential side cannot be an actual **object of vision**. The common candidate is therefore existence, shared by the Necessary Existent with contingent things. Hence God's visibility is possible.

An objection denies that the vision of a substance and of an accident are the same kind of possibility, or denies that one kind of phenomenon always needs one kind of cause: heat may arise from sun and fire. The response clarifies the **causal** language. What is sought is primarily the **kind of thing to which vision can relate** (*mutaʿallaq al-ruʾya*), not a physical producer of the ability to see. We can see a subject under a unified apprehension without judging whether it is a substance or an accident, or whether it is a man, horse, blackness or greenness; the **identity of the existent** is encountered before those detailed categorial judgements. A single visual apprehension of Zayd may be followed by a more detailed analysis of its bodily substances and accidents, or may occur without that analysis ever being considered. The actual object of sight is thus not the very accidentality or substantiality which separates those cases. It is the existent's reality under a more general condition.

Another objection says that existence might be the shared ground while a **special condition** belonging to creatures is needed to see them, or that the distinctive nature of the Necessary Existent prevents visibility. The proposed answer distinguishes conditions affecting the **occurrence** of sight from conditions affecting its **possibility**: to say that an existent can be seen is to say it is the appropriate kind of thing for such a relation; particular impediments may prevent actual sight without removing that possibility. Other objections deny that “existence” is a concept shared between God and creatures, returning to an earlier controversy about the identity of existence and essence. Even if the word has a common concept—the entity's having **a real identity**—one must not confuse that with saying the identities of God and creatures are one.

The argument has consequences its advocates acknowledge. If existence is sufficient for potential visibility, why should not **sounds, tastes, odours, thoughts, volitions, powers and other forms of cognition** be visible? They answer that these may indeed be **intrinsically capable of being seen**, although God's accustomed manner of producing our vision does not include seeing them. The opponent regards this as counterintuitive; the reply says strangeness is not contradiction. An attempt to reverse the proof by using **possibility of being created** fails because possible creaturehood is an abstract status, and **origination** is a suitable distinguishing ground for creaturehood although it is not an independently visible object. A more pointed counterexample from **tangibility** is judged powerful: applying the same common-existence reasoning to bodily touch yields consequences which are difficult to accept.

The author explicitly concedes that **the weakness of this proof is manifest**. It would also be wrong to claim that the visible object is **existence alone** and that differences among visible creatures are merely deduced; al-Rāzī rightly rejects that as contrary to evident experience. A stronger formulation is that **existence makes the particular individual essence capable of being seen**, not that the eye sees an abstract universal called existence and nothing else.

### The occurrence of vision: scriptural and transmitted arguments

Actual occurrence cannot be established by bare metaphysical argument; it depends on **transmission**. Sunni proponents invoke the early community's received belief, scriptural wording and prophetic reports. A report circulated by twenty-one major Companions is cited in support, though the author observes that specific reported traditions can remain **solitary reports** rather than indisputably mass transmitted in every chain.

The first Qurʾānic verse is **“Faces on that day radiant, looking to their Lord”** (Q 75:22–23). The verb *naẓara* joined to *ilā* is ordinarily read as **looking**, which either signifies visual apprehension or is its normal concomitant. It may literally mean turning the pupil toward a visible object in expectation of seeing; such bodily confrontation cannot apply to God, so one understands the expression as **vision** by an established figure. The order of the words may emphasize the Lord and complete the verse's cadence; alternatively it implies a rhetorical **restriction**, as though those absorbed in beholding the divine majesty scarcely look at anything else.

Opponents answer that *ilā* may be a **noun** meaning favour or bounty, not a preposition, and *naẓira* may mean **waiting for**, or that looking *to* someone can mean expecting favour from him. They adduce passages of poetry concerning expectant faces and the thirsty looking toward clouds. Moreover, “looking” need not entail **seeing**, since one may look at the moon without discerning it, and the Qurʾān itself speaks of persons looking without seeing. One might also posit an omitted object: “looking toward the **reward of** their Lord.” The replies say that the verse is an announcement of **joy already bestowed**; the fearful act of waiting for an expected benefit ill suits its depiction of fulfillment, especially when the expression expressly mentions faces and looking *to*. Making *ilā* a noun is strained, the poetic cases need not establish the supposed construction, and inserting an unexpressed object without a decisive indication is unwarranted.

Nevertheless the author is carefully qualified: **the verse alone does not yield demonstrative certainty eliminating every possible alternative interpretation**. The technical replies are more fully considered in al-Rāzī's *Nihāyat al-ʿUqūl*.

Another verse says that some will on that day be **“veiled from their Lord”** (Q 83:15). Since the unbelievers are singled out for veiling as a humiliation, it is inferred that believers are not veiled; to interpret the veil merely as exclusion from reward or honour is said to be less natural. Another verse promises **“the fairest and an increase”** (Q 10:26), which many exegetes interpret as Paradise and the **vision of God**. This is consistent, it is claimed, with describing the fairest as deserved recompense and the increase as a further grace. Even though vision is the highest honour, naming it an *increase* intimates that it is beyond the ordinary scale of rewards due for works.

Among prophetic traditions is the report: **“You will see your Lord as you see this full moon; you will not crowd one another in seeing Him.”** A narration from Ṣuhayb links the “increase” verse to the lifting of a veil before the people of Paradise, who find no gift dearer than gazing toward God. Another narration describes ranks of the people of Paradise, with the most honoured among them beholding the divine countenance morning and evening. Trusted specialists have accepted these reports, although the author cautions that they include reports classified as **āḥād**, which have a distinct epistemic status from mass-transmitted certainty.

### Rational objections from the opponents

The opponents' rational objections have three principal roots.

**(1) Confrontation and direction.** What is seen must be *opposite* the seer, either directly or, as they claim, through a mirror. Strictly speaking, in a mirror what is confronting the eye is the **reflected image**, not numerically the face represented by it. If confrontation were necessary for every vision, a visible God would occupy a spatial direction and region, and would have to be an independently spatial substance or an inhering accident. He would be within or outside the observer's body, within or outside Paradise, whole or part, finite or divisible, and at some distance or in physical contact. If all believers saw Him simultaneously, He would either be divided among their eyes or multiply; if they saw Him in succession despite equal perceptual powers, the unequal access would need a physical obstruction. If God were seen together with another object, the two visible objects would have to be spatially ordered; if not, objects normally seen in Paradise would mysteriously disappear from sight. These difficulties derive from treating confrontation as inseparable from seeing.

**Reply:** vision is an act of **perception which God creates** when He wishes and of whatever existent He wishes. Necessity cannot simply be invoked on a proposition opposed by many rational investigators. Even if ordinary worldly sight requires direction, a divine vision can differ from it either in **specific nature** or in **particular mode of occurrence**, with different prerequisites. To say it is *without modality* (*bilā kayf*) is to exclude the particular **spatial conditions and modes of bodily vision**, not to claim that the perception, the perceiver and what is perceived have no predicates whatever. An objector may fairly ask whether the resulting perception is still the **same sort of vision** originally disputed, rather than the fully disclosed knowledge accepted by the other side. The reply does not resolve this concern simply by changing names.

**(2) Emission of rays or reception of an image.** Sight is explained, on different theories, by a ray issuing from the eye to the object or a likeness impressed in the eye. Neither could apply to God's essence. **Reply:** these physiological theories are themselves disputed even among philosophers; moreover their conditions apply to corporeal sight in the world, and need not govern divine vision. Even an otherwise common general kind of perception may occur through different physical means.

**(3) Absence of impediments.** If a nonspatial divine object may be seen with a healthy visual faculty and no ordinary obstruction, God should be visible continually, **already in this world**, and perpetually in Paradise. The first is evidently false and the second conflicts with reports that people in Paradise engage in other pleasures. If visibility is possible and the eye healthy, why should seeing not follow? To make vision always contingent on God's freely creating it would allegedly allow enormous mountains and overwhelming sounds to be present unperceived despite normal perceptual conditions.

**Reply:** that scenario is **intrinsically possible** without being a reasonable belief about what is **actually present**. We possess ordinary certain knowledge that no such mountains stand before us, as we do that there is no sea of mercury or mountain of ruby in specified familiar surroundings. The natural certainty is not logically grounded in a universal necessity of perception upon physical conditions; it remains even in those who have never argued such a necessity. Further, seeing God in the afterlife might require a specially strengthened **perceptual capacity** given only then and only at certain times. It is weak to assume that an eye here and an eye hereafter, because both are called eyes, must share every necessary condition. Al-Rāzī challenges the completeness of the alleged sensory conditions from ordinary examples: a distant large body appears small, allegedly because some of its parts are seen but others not; dust is discernible in a cloud but not as dispersed minute grains. The replies distinguish distances of parts and the interdependence of perceptibility among grains; such counterexamples do not eliminate the possibility of further ordinary conditions.

### The strongest negative scriptural text: “Eyes do not apprehend Him”

The opponents appeal to **“Eyes do not apprehend Him, while He apprehends eyes”** (Q 6:103). They argue that apprehension by the eye is simply **seeing**, either as an identical notion or as its inseparable implication. The plural **al-abṣār**, when introduced by the article and under negation, gives a universal denial: no eyes apprehend Him. It would be false if believers eventually saw Him. They also argue that the negation occurs as divine **praise**, so the contrary—God's being seen—would be a deficiency and impossible.

The author introduces a lengthy logical and linguistic qualification: **negation in sentences with universal or restrictive phrases does not always take the same scope**. One can deny that **all** of a group acted (not all did), or assert of each member that it **did not** act (none did). The difference depends on whether the whole-group relation is formed before negating, or the negation is formed before being applied to the whole. Similar differences occur with adverbial qualifications, prepositional causes, and restrictive focus. “I did not strike him for discipline” might mean I struck him but from another motive, or I refrained from striking him **for a reason of honour**. “He did not come mounted” may indicate that he came on foot, whereas the qualification attached to the negation may designate why the action did not occur. Negative expressions with an indefinite term or restrictive focus must be analysed under this same distinction. Even the scope of conditionals, imperatives and their reasons may differ: a condition can specify the fact described or specify **why the statement is being made**. He insists that this is a fertile general principle insufficiently clarified in earlier treatments.

Despite recognizing scope distinctions, he grants that the verse's natural context does favor the **universal negative** reading. The strongest replies are therefore different.

**First:** a universal negative concerning all eyes need not be universal **for all times and conditions**; it can deny vision in this life. The objector argues that a divine quality of praise should endure forever. The answer distinguishes praise regarding God's **essence or intrinsic attributes**, which does not cease, from praise concerning what God **does or does not create**. The nonoccurrence of a created act of perception can end without any intrinsic alteration of the divine essence. Even if an all-time negation were the most readily apparent reading, mere apparentness would not give demonstrative certainty against other transmitted evidence.

**Second and preferable:** *idrāk* is **more specific than seeing**. It implies *reaching* or **comprehensively encompassing** the object, like overtaking another person. One can say, “I saw the moon but my eyes did not fully apprehend it,” if clouds obscure its aspect; one cannot normally say “my eyes fully apprehended it but I did not see it.” Thus *idrāk* may entail seeing, while seeing does not entail total *idrāk*. As “comprehension” is more than simple knowing, the negation of comprehensive perceptual grasp need not negate every kind of vision. To deny that God is encompassed and measured is manifestly praiseworthy. The response also explains “He apprehends the eyes” as God's complete knowing or seeing of the eyes. The claimed identity of seeing and apprehending is contested on grounds of usage, not merely by a scholastic stipulation.

**Third**, a reply attributed to al-Ashʿarī says that the text denies apprehension by **eyes as organs**, while the dispute concerns the **persons** who see. The author finds the literal formulation weak: what is normally called ocular seeing is attributed to people **through** their organs; distinguishing subject and instrument in this way would rob the verse of force. A more defensible intention is that it denies **bodily apprehension by physical confrontation and impression**, without excluding the nonspatial perception being disputed.

The Sunni side also sometimes attempts to deduce **possibility** from the praise that God is not seen: a negation of sight is praiseworthy only if sight is in principle possible, unlike the absence of vision in a sheer nonentity. The objection observes that God is praised for transcending creaturely limitations even when those limitations are impossible in His case. Some responses distinguish God from sounds, tastes and odours, whose visibility is absent by ordinary custom while they have obvious marks of created deficiency. The argument becomes delicate: to praise a Being of manifest perfection for being **unseen** can express majesty even though nonappearance is no intrinsic deficiency or separate perfection. This discussion also interacts with whether **takwīn** is a beginningless attribute or creation of vision is an originated act. The author indicates the conceptual difficulties rather than treating this proof as conclusive.

### Further negative scriptural arguments and their replies

**“You will not see Me”** (*lan tarānī*) is again adduced. Some take *lan* to deny forever; others hold it emphatically excludes future vision. The reply is that perpetual negation is not securely established as the intrinsic meaning of *lan*, and emphatic denial of **this** future occurrence does not entail every possible time. Its immediate context is the request to see God **in the present world**. Even an apparently general form must be interpreted in light of the full range of evidence.

Another text states that God speaks to human beings only **by inspiration**, **from behind a veil**, or **through a sent messenger** (Q 42:51). The opponent says this eliminates face-to-face seeing during God's speaking, which would make vision even less likely at other times. The reply says the verse classifies **the manners of divine communication**, not the spatial conditions of every encounter. Indeed, an immediate inspired communication need not be an encounter “behind a veil,” so the latter is not exhaustive of all ways revelation may accompany knowledge. Even if the verse had an implication against visible communication, the occasion and the specified prophetic worldly circumstances limit it. The author discusses the grammatical possibilities of *waḥyan* as an accusative of mode/source, “from behind a veil” as describing an implied speech, and “or send a messenger” as a coordinated infinitival construction or a separate circumstantial category.

A further argument observes that the Qurʾān rebukes certain people who demanded visible sight of God, describing them as **arrogant**, unjust and audacious, and mentions the thunderbolt that overtook those who demanded an open vision. If vision were permissible, why punish its request? **Reply:** the condemnation concerns **obstinate conditions imposed upon prophecy** or a demand to see God **in this life under the bodily conditions of direction and confrontation**, not the bare abstract possibility of another kind of sight. They were also rebuked for demands to have angels or a book sent down, things which are possible in themselves. Moses' declaration of repentance after the event can thus concern his **asking without prior permission**, or asking for vision in the present worldly condition, rather than a renunciation of its possibility forever. Reports of visual seeing during the Ascension are disputed; the majority, the author says, deny literal ocular seeing there and cite a report of **seeing with the heart**. Vision in dreams has been allowed by many earlier authorities, a further matter to be distinguished from bodily sight.

### Concluding question: can the attributes themselves be perceived?

Among those admitting a beatific vision, opinion differs on whether the **divine attributes** can be seen. The majority admit their *possible* visibility when accepting the proof that **every existent** is in principle visible, though no separate proof establishes that the attributes will actually be seen. Similar reasoning might be extended to **hearing, smell, taste and touch** if each is explained as a mode of cognition and if the common existence argument is valid. It is not disputed that God cannot be an **object smelled, tasted or physically touched**, for these descriptions belong to bodily objects and accidents. The only conceivable debate is whether a form of apprehension comparable to the information ordinarily obtained through these senses could occur **without bodily contact** and be related to a nonbodily existent. But once the weaknesses of the universal-existence argument and its unrestricted extension to the senses are acknowledged, the prudent course is to confine the discussion here to **vision**.

**Editorial assessment:** The author explicitly characterizes the general rational proof for visibility as weak and concedes that some transmitted readings cannot establish a **demonstratively certain** conclusion in isolation. The intended thesis is not that God acquires spatial location in order to be seen, nor that ordinary sensory physiology persists unchanged in the Hereafter. The dispute concerns whether there can be an irreducibly **perceptual** apprehension of the nonspatial divine reality, not merely knowledge of a proposition about God.

The actual object of sight is thus not the very accidentality or substantiality which separates those cases. It is the existent's reality under a more general condition.

Another objection says that existence might be the shared ground while a special condition belonging to creatures is needed to see them, or that the distinctive nature of the Necessary Existent prevents visibility. The proposed answer distinguishes conditions affecting the occurrence of sight from conditions affecting its possibility: to say that an existent can be seen is to say it is the appropriate kind of thing for such a relation; particular impediments may prevent actual sight without removing that possibility. Other objections deny that “existence” is a concept shared between God and creatures, returning to an earlier controversy about the identity of existence and essence. Even if the word has a common concept—the entity's having a real identity—one must not confuse that with saying the identities of God and creatures are one.

The argument has consequences its advocates acknowledge. If existence is sufficient for potential visibility, why should not sounds, tastes, odours, thoughts, volitions, powers and other forms of cognition be visible? They answer that these may indeed be intrinsically capable of being seen, although God's accustomed manner of producing our vision does not include seeing them. The opponent regards this as counterintuitive; the reply says strangeness is not contradiction. An attempt to reverse the proof by using possibility of being created fails because possible creaturehood is an abstract status, and origination is a suitable distinguishing ground for creaturehood although it is not an independently visible object. A more pointed counterexample from tangibility is judged powerful: applying the same common-existence reasoning to bodily touch yields consequences which are difficult to accept.

The author explicitly concedes that the weakness of this proof is manifest. It would also be wrong to claim that the visible object is existence alone and that differences among visible creatures are merely deduced; al-Rāzī rightly rejects that as contrary to evident experience. A stronger formulation is that existence makes the particular individual essence capable of being seen, not that the eye sees an abstract universal called existence and nothing else.

The occurrence of vision: scriptural and transmitted arguments

Actual occurrence cannot be established by bare metaphysical argument; it depends on transmission. Sunni proponents invoke the early community's received belief, scriptural wording and prophetic reports. A report circulated by twenty-one major Companions is cited in support, though the author observes that specific reported traditions can remain solitary reports rather than indisputably mass transmitted in every chain.

The first Qurʾānic verse is “Faces on that day radiant, looking to their Lord” (Q 75:22–23). The verb naẓara joined to ilā is ordinarily read as looking, which either signifies visual apprehension or is its normal concomitant. It may literally mean turning the pupil toward a visible object in expectation of seeing; such bodily confrontation cannot apply to God, so one understands the expression as vision by an established figure. The order of the words may emphasize the Lord and complete the verse's cadence; alternatively it implies a rhetorical restriction, as though those absorbed in beholding the divine majesty scarcely look at anything else.

Opponents answer that ilā may be a noun meaning favour or bounty, not a preposition, and naẓira may mean waiting for, or that looking to someone can mean expecting favour from him. They adduce passages of poetry concerning expectant faces and the thirsty looking toward clouds. Moreover, “looking” need not entail seeing, since one may look at the moon without discerning it, and the Qurʾān itself speaks of persons looking without seeing. One might also posit an omitted object: “looking toward the reward of their Lord.” The replies say that the verse is an announcement of joy already bestowed; the fearful act of waiting for an expected benefit ill suits its depiction of fulfillment, especially when the expression expressly mentions faces and looking to. Making ilā a noun is strained, the poetic cases need not establish the supposed construction, and inserting an unexpressed object without a decisive indication is unwarranted.

Nevertheless the author is carefully qualified: the verse alone does not yield demonstrative certainty eliminating every possible alternative interpretation. The technical replies are more fully considered in al-Rāzī's Nihāyat al-ʿUqūl.

Another verse says that some will on that day be “veiled from their Lord” (Q 83:15). Since the unbelievers are singled out for veiling as a humiliation, it is inferred that believers are not veiled; to interpret the veil merely as exclusion from reward or honour is said to be less natural. Another verse promises “the fairest and an increase” (Q 10:26), which many exegetes interpret as Paradise and the vision of God. This is consistent, it is claimed, with describing the fairest as deserved recompense and the increase as a further grace. Even though vision is the highest honour, naming it an increase intimates that it is beyond the ordinary scale of rewards due for works.

Among prophetic traditions is the report: “You will see your Lord as you see this full moon; you will not crowd one another in seeing Him.” A narration from Ṣuhayb links the “increase” verse to the lifting of a veil before the people of Paradise, who find no gift dearer than gazing toward God. Another narration describes ranks of the people of Paradise, with the most honoured among them beholding the divine countenance morning and evening. Trusted specialists have accepted these reports, although the author cautions that they include reports classified as āḥād, which have a distinct epistemic status from mass-transmitted certainty.

Rational objections from the opponents

The opponents' rational objections have three principal roots.

(1) Confrontation and direction. What is seen must be opposite the seer, either directly or, as they claim, through a mirror. Strictly speaking, in a mirror what is confronting the eye is the reflected image, not numerically the face represented by it. If confrontation were necessary for every vision, a visible God would occupy a spatial direction and region, and would have to be an independently spatial substance or an inhering accident. He would be within or outside the observer's body, within or outside Paradise, whole or part, finite or divisible, and at some distance or in physical contact. If all believers saw Him simultaneously, He would either be divided among their eyes or multiply; if they saw Him in succession despite equal perceptual powers, the unequal access would need a physical obstruction. If God were seen together with another object, the two visible objects would have to be spatially ordered; if not, objects normally seen in Paradise would mysteriously disappear from sight. These difficulties derive from treating confrontation as inseparable from seeing.

Reply: vision is an act of perception which God creates when He wishes and of whatever existent He wishes. Necessity cannot simply be invoked on a proposition opposed by many rational investigators. Even if ordinary worldly sight requires direction, a divine vision can differ from it either in specific nature or in particular mode of occurrence, with different prerequisites. To say it is without modality (bilā kayf) is to exclude the particular spatial conditions and modes of bodily vision, not to claim that the perception, the perceiver and what is perceived have no predicates whatever. An objector may fairly ask whether the resulting perception is still the same sort of vision originally disputed, rather than the fully disclosed knowledge accepted by the other side. The reply does not resolve this concern simply by changing names.

(2) Emission of rays or reception of an image. Sight is explained, on different theories, by a ray issuing from the eye to the object or a likeness impressed in the eye. Neither could apply to God's essence. Reply: these physiological theories are themselves disputed even among philosophers; moreover their conditions apply to corporeal sight in the world, and need not govern divine vision. Even an otherwise common general kind of perception may occur through different physical means.

(3) Absence of impediments. If a nonspatial divine object may be seen with a healthy visual faculty and no ordinary obstruction, God should be visible continually, already in this world, and perpetually in Paradise. The first is evidently false and the second conflicts with reports that people in Paradise engage in other pleasures. If visibility is possible and the eye healthy, why should seeing not follow? To make vision always contingent on God's freely creating it would allegedly allow enormous mountains and overwhelming sounds to be present unperceived despite normal perceptual conditions.

Reply: that scenario is intrinsically possible without being a reasonable belief about what is actually present. We possess ordinary certain knowledge that no such mountains stand before us, as we do that there is no sea of mercury or mountain of ruby in specified familiar surroundings. The natural certainty is not logically grounded in a universal necessity of perception upon physical conditions; it remains even in those who have never argued such a necessity. Further, seeing God in the afterlife might require a specially strengthened perceptual capacity given only then and only at certain times. It is weak to assume that an eye here and an eye hereafter, because both are called eyes, must share every necessary condition. Al-Rāzī challenges the completeness of the alleged sensory conditions from ordinary examples: a distant large body appears small, allegedly because some of its parts are seen but others not; dust is discernible in a cloud but not as dispersed minute grains. The replies distinguish distances of parts and the interdependence of perceptibility among grains; such counterexamples do not eliminate the possibility of further ordinary conditions.

The strongest negative scriptural text: “Eyes do not apprehend Him”

The opponents appeal to “Eyes do not apprehend Him, while He apprehends eyes” (Q 6:103). They argue that apprehension by the eye is simply seeing, either as an identical notion or as its inseparable implication. The plural al-abṣār, when introduced by the article and under negation, gives a universal denial: no eyes apprehend Him. It would be false if believers eventually saw Him. They also argue that the negation occurs as divine praise, so the contrary—God's being seen—would be a deficiency and impossible.

The author introduces a lengthy logical and linguistic qualification: negation in sentences with universal or restrictive phrases does not always take the same scope. One can deny that all of a group acted (not all did), or assert of each member that it did not act (none did). The difference depends on whether the whole-group relation is formed before negating, or the negation is formed before being applied to the whole. Similar differences occur with adverbial qualifications, prepositional causes, and restrictive focus. “I did not strike him for discipline” might mean I struck him but from another motive, or I refrained from striking him for a reason of honour. “He did not come mounted” may indicate that he came on foot, whereas the qualification attached to the negation may designate why the action did not occur. Negative expressions with an indefinite term or restrictive focus must be analysed under this same distinction. Even the scope of conditionals, imperatives and their reasons may differ: a condition can specify the fact described or specify why the statement is being made. He insists that this is a fertile general principle insufficiently clarified in earlier treatments.

Despite recognizing scope distinctions, he grants that the verse's natural context does favor the universal negative reading. The strongest replies are therefore different.

First: a universal negative concerning all eyes need not be universal for all times and conditions; it can deny vision in this life. The objector argues that a divine quality of praise should endure forever. The answer distinguishes praise regarding God's essence or intrinsic attributes, which does not cease, from praise concerning what God does or does not create. The nonoccurrence of a created act of perception can end without any intrinsic alteration of the divine essence. Even if an all-time negation were the most readily apparent reading, mere apparentness would not give demonstrative certainty against other transmitted evidence.

Second and preferable: idrāk is more specific than seeing. It implies reaching or comprehensively encompassing the object, like overtaking another person. One can say, “I saw the moon but my eyes did not fully apprehend it,” if clouds obscure its aspect; one cannot normally say “my eyes fully apprehended it but I did not see it.” Thus idrāk may entail seeing, while seeing does not entail total idrāk. As “comprehension” is more than simple knowing, the negation of comprehensive perceptual grasp need not negate every kind of vision. To deny that God is encompassed and measured is manifestly praiseworthy. The response also explains “He apprehends the eyes” as God's complete knowing or seeing of the eyes. The claimed identity of seeing and apprehending is contested on grounds of usage, not merely by a scholastic stipulation.

Third, a reply attributed to al-Ashʿarī says that the text denies apprehension by eyes as organs, while the dispute concerns the persons who see. The author finds the literal formulation weak: what is normally called ocular seeing is attributed to people through their organs; distinguishing subject and instrument in this way would rob the verse of force. A more defensible intention is that it denies bodily apprehension by physical confrontation and impression, without excluding the nonspatial perception being disputed.

The Sunni side also sometimes attempts to deduce possibility from the praise that God is not seen: a negation of sight is praiseworthy only if sight is in principle possible, unlike the absence of vision in a sheer nonentity. The objection observes that God is praised for transcending creaturely limitations even when those limitations are impossible in His case. Some responses distinguish God from sounds, tastes and odours, whose visibility is absent by ordinary custom while they have obvious marks of created deficiency. The argument becomes delicate: to praise a Being of manifest perfection for being unseen can express majesty even though nonappearance is no intrinsic deficiency or separate perfection. This discussion also interacts with whether takwīn is a beginningless attribute or creation of vision is an originated act. The author indicates the conceptual difficulties rather than treating this proof as conclusive.

Further negative scriptural arguments and their replies

“You will not see Me” (lan tarānī) is again adduced. Some take lan to deny forever; others hold it emphatically excludes future vision. The reply is that perpetual negation is not securely established as the intrinsic meaning of lan, and emphatic denial of this future occurrence does not entail every possible time. Its immediate context is the request to see God in the present world. Even an apparently general form must be interpreted in light of the full range of evidence.

Another text states that God speaks to human beings only by inspiration, from behind a veil, or through a sent messenger (Q 42:51). The opponent says this eliminates face-to-face seeing during God's speaking, which would make vision even less likely at other times. The reply says the verse classifies the manners of divine communication, not the spatial conditions of every encounter. Indeed, an immediate inspired communication need not be an encounter “behind a veil,” so the latter is not exhaustive of all ways revelation may accompany knowledge. Even if the verse had an implication against visible communication, the occasion and the specified prophetic worldly circumstances limit it. The author discusses the grammatical possibilities of waḥyan as an accusative of mode/source, “from behind a veil” as describing an implied speech, and “or send a messenger” as a coordinated infinitival construction or a separate circumstantial category.

A further argument observes that the Qurʾān rebukes certain people who demanded visible sight of God, describing them as arrogant, unjust and audacious, and mentions the thunderbolt that overtook those who demanded an open vision. If vision were permissible, why punish its request? Reply: the condemnation concerns obstinate conditions imposed upon prophecy or a demand to see God in this life under the bodily conditions of direction and confrontation, not the bare abstract possibility of another kind of sight. They were also rebuked for demands to have angels or a book sent down, things which are possible in themselves. Moses' declaration of repentance after the event can thus concern his asking without prior permission, or asking for vision in the present worldly condition, rather than a renunciation of its possibility forever. Reports of visual seeing during the Ascension are disputed; the majority, the author says, deny literal ocular seeing there and cite a report of seeing with the heart. Vision in dreams has been allowed by many earlier authorities, a further matter to be distinguished from bodily sight.

Concluding question: can the attributes themselves be perceived?

Among those admitting a beatific vision, opinion differs on whether the divine attributes can be seen. The majority admit their possible visibility when accepting the proof that every existent is in principle visible, though no separate proof establishes that the attributes will actually be seen. Similar reasoning might be extended to hearing, smell, taste and touch if each is explained as a mode of cognition and if the common existence argument is valid. It is not disputed that God cannot be an object smelled, tasted or physically touched, for these descriptions belong to bodily objects and accidents. The only conceivable debate is whether a form of apprehension comparable to the information ordinarily obtained through these senses could occur without bodily contact and be related to a nonbodily existent. But once the weaknesses of the universal-existence argument and its unrestricted extension to the senses are acknowledged, the prudent course is to confine the discussion here to vision.

Editorial assessment: The author explicitly characterizes the general rational proof for visibility as weak and concedes that some transmitted readings cannot establish a demonstratively certain conclusion in isolation. The intended thesis is not that God acquires spatial location in order to be seen, nor that ordinary sensory physiology persists unchanged in the Hereafter. The dispute concerns whether there can be an irreducibly perceptual apprehension of the nonspatial divine reality, not merely knowledge of a proposition about God.

# MQ-C05-017 — Fourth chapter, second investigation: can the divine essence be known in its very reality?

**Arabic source:** source characters 1203042–1207290, printed volume II pp.122–124. **Status:** close explanatory translation, print and clause audit outstanding.

The dispute concerns knowledge of God's **very essence as it is in itself** (*kunh al-ḥaqīqa*), not merely whether people can know that God exists or that certain attributes belong to Him. Many exacting investigators deny that human beings actually attain such essential knowledge, against the majority of theologians. Among the deniers, however, many allow that it **could** be granted to humans, whereas philosophers are reported to deny even its possibility.

### Why the essence is said not to be known in its entirety

The deniers offer two grounds. **First**, what human beings know concerning God comprises His **existence**, meaning that He is actually existent rather than nonexistent; His **affirmative attributes**, such as being living, knowing and powerful; His **negative attributes**, such as being one, beginningless, endless, and neither body nor accident; and His **relations**, such as being Creator and Provider. These do not amount to apprehending the **specific intrinsic essence**. To say, as some investigators do, that existence is identical with the essence does not settle this objection: knowing **that** the essence exists is not the same as grasping its own particular existence as it really is. The corresponding point applies to attributes.

**Second**, God's specific essence is a **numerically particular reality**, and its complete apprehension must make the conception of sharing it by several individuals impossible. Yet the things we grasp regarding God can be represented in common concepts. We consequently need a demonstration of **uniqueness**, which would be redundant if the essence itself had already been grasped in its unshareable individuality. It is sometimes said that the concept Necessary Existent is universal even though there cannot be several instances of it: that claim concerns the **concept** of necessary existence, not the concrete essence denoted by it.

Two objections follow. Who can assert that the highest knowledge possessed by **every human** is limited to these abstract properties? That would presuppose complete knowledge of the cognitive attainments of every human being. Further, once one includes **unity proved demonstratively** among the known properties, several individuals cannot actually share those properties. The reply says that the **concept considered as concept** remains universal—even where an actual second individual is impossible. The author then clarifies a distinction that weakens the second original argument: the topic is grasp of divine **quiddity or specific nature**, not merely the divine **individuality**. Those denying grasp of the essence say it cannot be obtained by a **definition** (*ḥadd*) because the divine reality has no composite genus and differentia, and not by a **description** (*rasm*) because a description supplies signs rather than quiddity. They do not merely argue that an individual cannot be known through generic definitions. Supporters of attainable knowledge maintain that God's essence is nothing more than His being a necessarily existent reality necessarily qualified by knowledge, power, life, hearing, vision and other perfections. Some Muʿtazilites called the **Mashāyikhiyya** are reported to have claimed that they know God's very essence as He knows it, without degree of difference—a striking position distinct from the less ambitious majority argument.

### The controversy over *māʾiyya* and *khāṣṣiyya*

In kalām this is sometimes called the question of **māʾiyya**, with the doctrine attributed to **Ḍirār**, who maintained that God has a *whatness* known only to Himself and would be seen under that whatness if seen; divine power could give creatures a sixth sense to perceive the distinctive divine *whatness* and property. A report of similar language from Abū Ḥanīfa was strongly rejected by his followers. The risk is **assimilation to created kinds**: *māʾiyya* is sometimes understood as answering “What is it?” with a genus, and God has no genus. A member of a genus shares a general nature with other things, implying resemblance; that cannot be accepted for God.

A gentler interpretation takes the doctrine to say that God knows Himself by a kind of **immediate presence**, whereas humans know Him by proofs and reports, and that immediate perception gives knowledge not possessed by those lacking it. On this explanation no shared genus or extra entity called *māʾiyya* is posited. Our theologians therefore often prefer the term **distinctive property** (*khāṣṣiyya*), the specific reality not grasped by us now. The Qāḍī reportedly hesitates whether it will be known after the beatific vision in Paradise, out of caution against corporeal comparison.

### Does successful predication require full essential knowledge?

Those affirming human grasp of God's essence argue that we apply many true predicates and judgments to it. Judgment requires a conception of its **subject**; therefore the essence is known. Even saying “God's essence is unknown” seems to require knowing what one predicates ignorance of. The answer distinguishes **knowing the essence under a conception**, such as “the reality of the Necessary Existent,” from **grasping the very reality which satisfies that conception**. The former is an accidental or relational aspect, just like general words *essence*, *reality* and *quiddity*. It suffices for meaningful judgment without granting the disputed knowledge of the thing in its own innermost nature.

### Is such complete knowledge at least possible?

Philosophers offer two reasons against even its possibility. **First**, they hold that knowing a thing requires its **form or universal quiddity** to be represented in the soul, abstracted from its external individuating conditions, so that if the form were instantiated externally it would be that thing. The Necessary Existent has no universal quiddity admitting further individuation. Were such a form copied into several minds, it is alleged that the Necessary would become multiple and divine unity would fail. **Reply:** the thesis that every cognition is by an impressed form is not established; even if accepted for other objects, why extend it to knowing God or God's knowledge of Himself? Moreover, a multiplicity of **mental representations** is not a plurality of actual necessarily existing individuals. The unity of the external necessary being is not refuted by several concepts or likenesses in minds.

**Second**, cognition of quiddity is supposed to arise either immediately by **self-evidence**, by **definition** from genus and differentia, or by **description**. Divine knowledge by ordinary self-evidence is not granted; God is not a genus-and-differentia composite; and description gives properties rather than the very essence. **Reply:** that list need not exhaust ways of apprehension. Knowledge might be obtained by **inspiration**, by God's giving immediate knowledge of something ordinarily learned discursively, or by the soul's apprehending things directly when separated from its body, as has been discussed concerning immaterial realities. Even a description may serve as a route to a later insight into the thing itself, although it does not logically guarantee such an insight.

*Technical point:* The investigation distinguishes (1) knowing a proposition about God, (2) knowing the **concept** of necessary existence, (3) identifying the **unique individual** who satisfies it, and (4) grasping the **intrinsic divine quiddity**. These must not be rendered by one undifferentiated sense of “knowing God.”

title: Divine acts, first investigation: human actions, divine production and acquisition
en:
## The question and the proper sense in which an action is attributed to a human being

The fifth chapter concerns His acts, and contains several investigations. The first concerns **the creation of the acts of servants**: is God's creation of the voluntary actions of human beings—and indeed of other living things—among His acts? There is agreement that these actions are *their* actions, not God's, in the sense that it is the human being who stands, sits, eats or drinks, even if the action is created by God. For an action is truly attributed to the one in whom it occurs, not simply to whoever brings it into existence. Thus a body is white, although God creates and brings about its whiteness. It is little wonder, the author remarks sharply, that some unlearned Qadarites overlook this distinction and censure their opponents in public; it is more surprising that learned representatives of the school overlook it in their books. Scriptural ascriptions of acts to servants do not by themselves establish the disputed proposition, namely that the servant's act occurs **through his own power as its creator**.

The dispute is stated, as in *al-Mawāqif*, in several forms. On our view, the servant's act occurs **through God's power alone**. According to the Muʿtazila it occurs through the servant's power alone. According to al-Ustādh it occurs through both powers jointly, each pertaining to the underlying act. According to al-Qāḍī, divine power pertains to the underlying act and the human power to its character as obedience or disobedience. According to the philosophers, it takes place through a power God creates in the servant. The Muʿtazila do not dispute that God creates the servant's power; their language that He creates powers and capacities is widespread. Consequently the often proposed distinction between them and the philosophers is not well drawn. It is said that, for the Muʿtazila, the servant's power itself acts, whereas on the philosophers' doctrine divine power produces the servant's power, which in turn produces the act. Al-Rāzī and some Muʿtazilites instead distinguish voluntary, non-necessitating human production from the philosophical doctrine in which God necessarily bestows the power and will and these necessarily yield the effect. But possibility is predicated of power considered in itself; once complete power and will are present, the effect is necessary, and that necessity need not exclude choice. The learned author of *Qawāʿid al-ʿaqāʾid* accordingly reports the view as shared by the philosophers and Muʿtazila. A distinction remains between the Muʿtazilite account of God's voluntary bestowal of powers and the philosophers' account of their necessary occurrence upon the completion of the relevant disposition.

A further historical correction is required. It is commonly said that Imām al-Ḥaramayn held that a servant's act occurs through his power and will, as philosophers maintain. Yet this conflicts with the writings of his that al-Taftāzānī has seen. In the *Irshād* he states that the imams of the early community agreed, before the spread of innovations, that **God alone is Creator** and that every originated event arises through divine power, whether or not a created power is related to it. A property may relate to something without producing it, as knowledge relates to its object and desire may relate to another's act. Therefore a created power need not produce the object to which it relates.
