title: The first rational argument: possibility and the concurrence of powers
en:
**First rational argument.** The servant's act is a *possible* existent. Everything possible is within God's power, as established in the investigation on divine attributes. Therefore the servant's act falls under God's power. If it also belonged to the servant's power **as a producer independently efficacious**, there would be two independently complete efficient causes of a single effect. That impossibility was argued in the treatment of causes.

It is objected: the universality of divine power only establishes that a servant's act is within divine capacity—meaning that it could be produced by it in itself—not that this act actually occurs through divine power. The actuality could belong instead to human power. The reply is that if the act may be produced by divine power even while it actually occurs through created power, it would follow that the jointly impossible concurrence of independently producing causes is itself possible. Yet al-Taftāzānī adds **'there is a difficulty in this'** (*wa-fīhi naẓar*), warning that the argument has not yet been fully secured.

Al-Rāzī supplies a composite proof that every possible existent occurs through divine power. Possibility makes an effect dependent upon a cause. This cannot be a wholly indeterminate cause, for what is indeterminate has no concrete external realization and cannot produce an existent. Hence there must be some determinate cause. Possibility is one meaning found in all possible things, so all must depend upon that cause. A cause on which every possible depends cannot itself be possible; it must be necessary. Everything is accordingly brought about by its production. Since this necessary cause has been proved to be a voluntary agent and not a necessitating nature, all is said to occur through its power and choice. This is **al-Rāzī's argument as reported**, not an unqualified proof adopted without scrutiny.

Al-Rāzī also argues that anything within God's power must occur through **His power alone**. If it did not, either it would occur through another power alone—selecting one among supposedly equivalent independent powers, indeed selecting the weaker over the stronger divine power—or through both together, which would repeat the impossibility of jointly independent sufficient causes; or through neither, contrary to the stipulated actuality of the act. He adds that a sufficient cause's failure would require an impediment, which could only be the competing causal production, generating the same contradiction. If another independently produces what God could produce, God could no longer create that already existent thing; the creature would, it is argued, have made the divine power ineffective. In contrast, divine production of the action manifests the efficacy of divine power rather than frustrating it.

title: Rational arguments two to four: knowledge of actions, determining motives, and divine foreknowledge
en:
**Second argument: knowledge of the action's particulars.** If the servant were the independent producer of his acts, he would know their particulars. Production of this rather than another quantity, arrangement or manner needs specification by an intention, and intentional specification presupposes cognition of the intended detail. This is why the absence of the producer's knowledge is treated as surprising in the scriptural question, 'Does the one who created not know?' and why a wise artifact is adduced as evidence of its maker's knowledge. But human agents lack many details of the very deeds they perform. Someone asleep can carry out acts without recognizing their precise quantity or quality. A walker traverses a particular distance within a particular time without knowing every intervening stretch and place, every instant, pause, or degree of speed and slowness. A speaker pronounces definite letters in a definite order without knowing the precise anatomical instruments and their positions required to articulate them. A writer produces letters and words by moving the fingers without knowing the exact bones, cartilages, nerves, muscles and ligaments, nor the minute motions and placements by which the shapes are drawn. The putative producer thus lacks the exhaustive knowledge supposedly implied by independent origination.

**Third argument: action and omission require a determiner.** If the servant acts by independently effective power and full choice, he must be capable of either acting or refraining. Otherwise his deed would be compelled, not optional. Yet the preference of one side of the possible alternative either has a *preponderating determinant* (*murajjiḥ*) or does not. If it does not, one possible side obtains without a determiner; this undercuts the way an effect is used to prove the Creator and makes the outcome a matter of mere coincidence rather than personal choice. If it does have a determiner, and that determiner arises from the servant, the same question must be asked about its arising, leading either to a regress or to a determinant that is not the servant's own production. In the latter case, what finally determines the act comes from elsewhere. What has become outweighed cannot occur in preference to the superior alternative, and the possible does not become actual without attaining the requisite necessity. Thus the servant is not independently self-determining.

But al-Taftāzānī expressly limits this conclusion. It **challenges the Muʿtazilite conjunction of complete human independence with an uncoerced act**; it does not, by itself, prove that human agents have no productive role at all. He records four objections.

1. The argument opposes what is necessarily experienced: we plainly recognize our power and choice, and that we act if we wish and refrain if we wish.
2. Applied to the divine act it would make God a necessary cause rather than a free agent. If the complete conditions of production existed eternally, the world would be eternal. If something required was missing, its coming to exist would itself demand an explanation and the regress would end in an eternal condition whose effect was necessary.
3. A chooser can select between equal options, as when a fugitive takes one of two paths or a thirsty person chooses one of two cups. Will is a principle of preference and specification. One should distinguish an agent's *giving preference without a further determiner* from the inexplicable *obtaining of preference without any determining principle*.
4. A determinant not independently produced by the servant may be the conjunction of will with a fully developed motive. The act's necessity, considered in relation to this conjunction, need not abolish choice or the servant's capacity for acting and refraining considered simply as power.

The responses are likewise distinguished. To the first: the issue is not the ordinary conditional claim 'if I will, I act,' but whether the **willing and motive themselves** come about by our choice. Scripture says that human willing is subject to divine willing; some investigators therefore say that the upshot is compulsion even though choice appears at the immediate level—human beings are constrained in the guise of choosers. To the second: divine will is eternal and specifies an act's occurrence at its appointed time, requiring no newly originated determinant, whereas human volition arises successively in connection with particular new motives. To the third: the argument is binding only on Muʿtazilites who themselves insist that a determiner is required for choosing; it cannot simply be imposed on those who affirm free selection even between equivalent options or against the apparently preferable option. Al-Taftāzānī nevertheless questions whether such selection ever occurs without an actual motive, and replies to the fourth objection by emphasizing the necessity attached to that fully developed motive.

**Fourth argument: divine knowledge of future particulars.** God knows the particulars of what has been and what will be, and cannot be ignorant. Whatever God knows will occur must occur; whatever He knows will not occur cannot occur—**relative to His knowledge**, though the event may remain possible when considered in its own essence. A servant cannot fully choose between acting and refraining if one alternative is already necessary or impossible in this sense. The opponent replies that God can know precisely that an action takes place through human power and choice. The answer is that its occurring through that power and choice would then be assured, such that the alternative decision could not occur. This is the intended denial of independent, fully self-determining choice; it does not without further reasoning demonstrate the complete absence of human production. Al-Taftāzānī notes again that some arguments aim at dialectical constraint rather than conclusively proving the proposition.

An objection turns this same reasoning against God's own free action. The response distinguishes divine eternal will, whose timeless relation specifies the act's occurrence in time, from temporal human volitions. Al-Rāzī elsewhere argues that the eternal necessity of a future deed needs an eternal ground: it cannot arise from a contingent creature and cannot be divine knowledge as mere correspondence to its object, so it must be divine power and will. The author judges this particular proof **very weak**. An analogous argument from divine will—that God either wills a human act and it must occur, or does not and it cannot occur—is met by two Muʿtazilite objections: God need not will either alternative, and it is not granted on their theory that everything God wills a servant to do necessarily occurs.

title: The fifth argument, additional arguments, and the first scriptural proofs of divine creation
en:
**Fifth rational argument: incompatible determinations.** Suppose a servant could independently produce his act. He wills a body to move at a given instant while God wills it to be at rest. Both wishes cannot be realized together. Nor can both fail, since a body after its first instant cannot be devoid of both motion and rest, and because failure of either independently sufficient cause would require an impediment—here the occurrence of the other's object. If neither occurred, their respective impediments would both need to occur, again a contradiction. If only one occurs, one of two equally independent productive powers would have prevailed without a determining advantage. The opponent says that God's object occurs because His power is stronger: independence does not mean equal strength. Al-Rāzī replies that the object of power is not divisible into degrees of power, so greater extent of God's power does not necessarily mean a greater intensity of power over this particular object. The author notes that this response has an evident weakness.

**Further traditional proofs are reported but not simply endorsed.** If the servant possessed independent originating power, he could reproduce his act, since the original possibility of producing it does not vanish with time. Yet the opponents deny our power to restore an annihilated act. If one can produce a particular act, one should be able to reproduce another exactly like it; however, no amount of care enables us invariably to reproduce all the details of an earlier act. Moreover, if the sufficient condition for being producible is possibility or origination, and production means conferring existence, human power should extend to every possible body and accident, an unacceptable consequence. Human acquisitive power is said not to be subject to this argument because it relates to particulars and their conditions, which differ.

Another argument judges that human faith, obedience and beneficent acts are, in important respects, nobler than some created bodies, harmful creatures and painful accidents. If a person created the former independently, his acts would surpass God's in excellence. The opponent argues that the capacity for faith, itself given by God, is nobler than the act that depends on it. The rejoinder exposes the opposite implication: the capacity for evil would then have to be worse than evil itself. Further, the community agrees that a person may pray to God for faith and obedience and for protection against disbelief and disobedience, and ought to praise God for the gift of faith itself—not merely for the preliminaries of capacity, opportunity, direction and assistance. If God did not create the acts, such prayers and gratitude would, it is argued, lack their proper object.

The resulting question is how to speak about 'created faith'. A cited legal opinion censures the bare proposition 'faith is created', whereas the rival theories dispute whether faith is created by God or by a servant. Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī is invoked to explain the distinction: neither absolute compulsion nor independent Qadarite creation is intended. **From God** come instruction, enabling grace, guidance and the gift, related to *takwīn*; **from the servant** come recognition, intending, being guided and accepting, which are originated. The author prefers correcting an injudicious formulation in the book rather than preserving it as a source of confusion. He then explicitly acknowledges **several weaknesses in the additional rational arguments**. The safer recourse, he says, is Scripture, transmitted tradition and the consensus of the people of truth. This does not mean that consensus alone establishes a philosophical fact such as the world's temporal origination or the Maker's beginninglessness. It means that their agreement indicates a conclusive basis for their doctrine, even if its precise proof has not been reconstructed here.

**The objection to using revelation.** Scriptural evidence, it is argued, presupposes the truthfulness of divine and prophetic statements and the evidentiary force of miracles. Yet if God creates every evil, and no act is morally repugnant when ascribed to God, one seems unable to exclude deception, false speech or a miracle granted to an impostor. The reply treats the established expectation that these possibilities do not occur as part of the ordinary certainties analogous to necessary knowledge. Moreover, the current appeal to Scripture is *ad hominem* against opponents who already accept its authority and cite it to reject God's production of evil and of human actions. If their use of Scripture presupposed the very thesis they are trying to establish, their own appeal would be circular.

## Scriptural indications using the language of creation

The author classifies revealed proofs by their different expressions: creation of everything, creation specifically of human works, divine *making*, divine *doing*, and other constructions. He begins with formulas in which God is praised as 'Creator of everything' (for example, Q 6:102 and 13:16) and the denial that God has any partner, followed by the assertion that He has created everything (Q 25:2). The force of the general expression is disputed. The Necessary Being is excluded from 'everything' by rational necessity, not by an arbitrary exception that would undermine the general statement. The fact that God does not count Himself among the things He creates is comparable to the conventional restriction of 'everyone who entered the house' when the speaker says that he honored everyone who entered. The additional words 'He created everything' after denying any partner in dominion prevent the rival suggestion that human beings create some particular things while not being God's comprehensive partners.

He then examines Q 54:49, **«إنا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر»**. The preferred accusative *kulla shayʾin* supports a construction 'We created every thing according to a measure', while the hypothetical nominative would more easily permit the restricted claim 'Every thing that We created is measured'. Fifth rational argument: incompatible determinations. Suppose a servant could independently produce his act. He wills a body to move at a given instant while God wills it to be at rest. Both wishes cannot be realized together. Nor can both fail, since a body after its first instant cannot be devoid of both motion and rest, and because failure of either independently sufficient cause would require an impediment—here the occurrence of the other's object. If neither occurred, their respective impediments would both need to occur, again a contradiction. If only one occurs, one of two equally independent productive powers would have prevailed without a determining advantage. The opponent says that God's object occurs because His power is stronger: independence does not mean equal strength. Al-Rāzī replies that the object of power is not divisible into degrees of power, so greater extent of God's power does not necessarily mean a greater intensity of power over this particular object. The author notes that this response has an evident weakness.

If the servant possessed independent originating power, he could reproduce his act, since the original possibility of producing it does not vanish with time. Some texts say expressly that God is *the Creator*, yet their indication of exclusive creatorship requires syntactical precision. In **«هو الله الخالق»**, if *al-Khāliq* is the predicate, and the preceding pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*) or is explained by the divine name, the construction expresses a restriction of the title to God. If *al-Khāliq* is an adjective, al-Rāzī attempts to reach the same conclusion through a syntactic argument about the proper name *Allāh*. Al-Taftāzānī calls that explanation weak to anyone acquainted with the usages of speech.

In **«وأسروا قولكم أو اجهروا به إنه عليم بذات الصدور ألا يعلم من خلق»** (Q 67:13–14), God's knowledge of inner intentions, aversions, beliefs and thoughts is argued for on the basis of His creating them. This resembles establishing the consequence (knowledge) by establishing its supposed prerequisite (creation). One may reverse the reasoning: since human beings do not know all the detailed effects of what they do, they cannot be the independent creators of those effects. Yet the author questions two premises. Are the inner contents of the breast, especially all such passing states, the very *voluntary actions* that form the subject of the dispute? And does knowledge follow universally from all creation considered in abstraction, or specifically from a Creator who is the Subtle and All-Aware? These qualifications must not be suppressed.

**«هل من خالق غير الله يرزقكم من السماء والأرض»** (Q 35:3) denies another *creator who provides sustenance from heaven and earth*, rather than explicitly denying every possible sense of creator irrespective of qualification. Al-Rāzī tries to infer the broader denial by considering the angels mediating rainfall as providers in the way a king may be said to provide someone with a livelihood. Al-Taftāzānī finds this weak. Conversely, **«والذين يدعون من دون الله لا يخلقون شيئا»** (Q 16:20) could include living beings invoked by unbelievers—such as Jesus or angels—not only inanimate idols, and **«هذا خلق الله فأروني ماذا خلق الذين من دونه»** (Q 31:11) would invite opponents to show some made motions and shapes as counterexamples if human beings were creators. These latter readings depend, however, on the relative terms not referring exclusively to idols. Other verses about God's creation and command and His giving every thing its creation and guidance are treated as evidence of the same kind.

Some opponents distinguish the title *creator* from an agent who merely *produces* an act: *khalq*, they say, is production according to an accurate pre-arranged measure, whereas a human deed can be defective or at odds with its intended result. The reply is that *khalq* signifies giving actuality according to some determined measure. Some human deeds also satisfy that description, so if the servant originated them he would indeed create them in this sense.

Other proofs use **divine making** (*jaʿl*). In the supplication **«واجعلنا مسلمين لك»** (Q 2:128), a verb governing two objects has the sense of turning something from one condition into another. When the result expressed as the second object is a human religious act, the wording presents that condition as produced by God. The Muʿtazila interpret such language as assistance, grace, abandonment or the creation of conditions and capacities, not direct creation of the resulting act. The author replies that the number and plainness of the occurrences make such wholesale reinterpretation difficult. Similarly, expressions such as **«فعال لما يريد»** (Q 85:16) are taken to mean that God brings about all that His will pertains to, including faith and obedience. Restricting this to 'He does whatever *act of His own* He wishes to perform' is an additional interpretive limitation.

In **«قل كل من عند الله»** (Q 4:78), which answers those who attribute good to God and misfortune to the Prophet, the text as interpreted here extends divine creation and will to all good and bad. Both classes share contingency and origination; the same need for a producer applies to each. The immediately following verse **«ما أصابك من حسنة فمن الله وما أصابك من سيئة فمن نفسك»** (Q 4:79) is then distinguished from creation: it can express the human's responsibility as a **secondary cause or occasion**, not independent production. The author also notes another possible rhetorical construal. Verses attributing blessings to God, describing His creative 'Be!', stating that He has inscribed faith in hearts, that He makes people laugh and weep, and that He makes humans travel by land and sea are likewise understood as including events that are ordinarily described as voluntary actions. Even the holding of birds in the air is mentioned as a case in which an animal's movement is attributed to divine production. Prayers for an expanded breast, victory and guidance of hearts show the same practical dependence. The author's position is that the rival readings are deviations from the apparent meaning without necessity if the opposing demonstrations fail.

## The reports concerning *qaḍāʾ* and *qadar*

The traditions on divine decree and the dependence of things upon divine willing are so numerous, he says, that even if individual reports are isolated in their transmission, their common meaning is widely transmitted (*mutawātir maʿnawī*). He compares the cumulative assurance to what is historically known of ʿAlī's courage or Ḥātim's generosity, and invokes compilers including al-Bukhārī and Muslim without asserting that every textual detail in every collection is identical.

He cites the exchange of Adam and Moses, in which Adam answers Moses' complaint about humanity's loss of Paradise by referring to God's decree before his own creation; the statement that one does not attain faith without believing in resurrection and both the good and evil of decree; and the report that everything, even incapacity and resourcefulness, is by decree. Another cited report says that God makes every maker and what he makes. The reports concerning hearts being between two fingers of the Merciful are invoked with the Prophet's prayer for steadfastness. In the version attributed to Jābir, the Prophet explains that hearts are turned by God, and an accompanying gesture is recorded in the source. These reports are used as a family of arguments for divine origination and guidance; **their precise transmission and grading remain for the independent ḥadīth apparatus**.

At this point the author turns from the Sunnī proofs to **Muʿtazilite arguments for human production of voluntary actions**. He distinguishes those following Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī, who treat the proposition as immediately known, from earlier Muʿtazilites who argue to it demonstratively.

title: Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī on the alleged immediacy of human production
en:
Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī and his followers assert that human beings produce their acts by their own power in a way that is **necessarily or immediately known** (*ḍarūrī*), planted in the minds of reasonable and impartial persons not bound by imitation of their predecessors. Their six considerations are offered either as reminders of an immediate cognition or as proofs that a judgement belongs to the class of necessary cognition—for even when a judgement is immediate, establishing that it is immediate may require argument.

**First**, everyone distinguishes at once between voluntary movements, such as walking and climbing a mountain, and involuntary movements, such as trembling or falling from a roof. The difference is that the first comes through the person's own power and production whereas the second does not. **Second**, we necessarily recognize the conformity of our conduct to intentions and motives: severe hunger brings a person to eat or drink, while knowledge that the food or water is poisoned prevents it. A voluntary producer is precisely one whose action comes about in agreement with such motives. **Third**, a reasonable person immediately finds it appropriate to praise a benefactor and blame someone who has injured him. That would not make sense if he did not recognize the person as the producer of the deed; one blames the stone-thrower, not the stone. **Fourth**, it is reasonable to command someone physically able to stand or walk, not a paralyzed person who cannot do either. The distinction presupposes the former's capacity to produce those actions, and if the judgement about the command is immediate the foundation of the judgement is said to be more immediate still. **Fifth**, we know that we can move a clod of earth but not a mountain; even a donkey attempts to jump a narrow ditch and not one impossibly wide. **Sixth**, the intelligent petitioner solicits what he believes the addressee can bring about, adopts means to obtain that deed, prohibits what the person can cause but what he dislikes, and makes wishes or expresses amazement concerning possible actions. All of these linguistic and practical forms, the opponent says, imply human origination.

The **reply** grants what these examples establish and denies the more ambitious inference. Some actions attributable to persons are dependent upon their powers, intentions, volitions and motives, whereas others are not. These are exactly the differences between voluntary and involuntary acts. Their being **objects of created power, performed by acquisition and following their intention**, even if God has created the power and the will, is adequate to explain praise, blame, requesting, prohibition, wishing and wondering. None of that shows that the agent is the **independent creator** of the attained action, which is the actual matter in dispute; still less does it prove that independent creatorship is known necessarily.

Al-Taftāzānī here sharply criticizes Abū al-Ḥusayn for effectively accusing all his learned opponents of denying what is immediately given. Some other Qadarites themselves consider the judgement demonstrative rather than necessary. Al-Rāzī, in the *Nihāyat al-ʿuqūl*, offers a further polemical explanation: Abū al-Ḥusayn maintained, against other Muʿtazilites, that an act requires a motive and that once the motive is complete the act necessarily follows. The combination of these propositions seemed to undermine the independently self-determining power central to the Muʿtazilite position. On al-Rāzī's report, Abū al-Ḥusayn therefore intensified his claim that human production is immediately known.

A possible defence distinguishes between **human power's causal relevance** and **its complete independence**. The need for a motive may disprove independence without disproving all contribution of created power. Al-Rāzī replies that it is precisely independence that his argument seeks to refute. Once the occurrence of the act is inevitable upon a motive and volition the servant does not independently produce, the Muʿtazilite moral objections to the creation of acts return: why is it supposed more coherent to command a servant to do what inevitably follows upon divinely produced motives than to command him concerning what God directly produces? Likewise, why would one be morally different if God punished a person for what was produced in him, instead of what inevitably followed on something God produced in him? Al-Rāzī pushes the same charge against the attribution of ugly or unjust acts. **This is al-Rāzī's polemical argument as reported; it should not be silently identified with every Muʿtazilite's self-description.**

Later Muʿtazilites are reported to explain 'necessity upon the completion of motive' in a softer sense: one can know that an agent will do something with a completely available alternative, much as one can know that God will reward prophets and saints and punish unbelievers even though these results are not intrinsically impossible to omit. They cite the Arabs' inability to match the Qurʾān: if they had both power and sufficiently compelling motives, they would have produced something comparable. The author replies that either the completed motive **necessitates the act**, in which case the servant cannot withhold it at that moment and the opponent's denial of independence fails, or it does not necessitate it, in which case calling the consequence 'necessary' and inferring its occurrence from the motive are unwarranted. The argument that the challengers would have produced a match had they possessed the capacity depends upon the conditional entailment; without it the argument cannot establish incapacity from failure. The next discussion turns to the **five older Muʿtazilite rational arguments** for independent production.

title: The five rational Muʿtazilite arguments and the distinction between attribution and creation
en:
The older Muʿtazilites consider the assertion that human beings independently produce their actions not immediately evident but established by **five arguments**, rational and scriptural. The first and chief rational argument adduces several supposedly unacceptable results of the opposing doctrine.

**(1a) Praise and blame would be invalid.** What sense is there in praising or blaming someone for what is not his act and has not occurred through his power and choice? The reply denies the premise. A subject may be praised or blamed in respect of a condition **belonging to it**, even if it does not produce that condition: beauty or ugliness, bodily proportion or excessive shortness furnish analogies.

**(1b) Command and prohibition would become meaningless.** It would be absurd to demand an action not within the addressee's capacity, like commanding a human to create a living creature or fly to heaven, or even commanding a stone to walk across the earth. Likewise, rewarding or punishing an agent for what the rewarder or punisher has produced would be senseless. The opponents press the point polemically: a being punishing creatures for acts that He created in them might seem more injurious than Satan, who merely incites and embellishes evil.

**(1c) Revelation and moral education would have no purpose.** If created power and choice produce nothing, promises and threats, prophetic missions, scriptures, inducement toward perfection and warnings against vice would, it is argued, achieve nothing. **(1d) Distinctions of moral and religious merit would collapse.** On that account the difference between faith and disbelief, beneficence and oppression, prophetic guidance and Satanic temptation, uttering prayers and uttering obscenities would vanish if every event were simply God's creation without any creaturely efficacy. **(1e) Voluntary and compelled bodily motion would be indistinguishable.** One plainly recognizes the difference between moving one's own hand and having it moved by another person.

title: Muʿtazilite scriptural arguments, the antinomies of the debate, and decree
en:
Al-Taftāzānī reports five principal **Muʿtazilite types of scriptural evidence** that human action belongs to the human agent.

**First**, innumerable verses ascribe actions directly to humans, from the description of people who believe in the unseen and establish prayer near the start of the Qurʾān, to the final sūrah's reference to one who whispers into human breasts. The author maintains that ascription itself is not disputed. Al-Rāzī is said to resolve the apparent tension by taking the **conjunction of created power and determining motive** as causally operative in the deed, while God is the Creator of that total conjunction. The action is therefore genuinely humanly ascribed without being independently created by the servant.

**Second**, Scripture commands and prohibits, praises faith and obedience, condemns disbelief and disobedience, promises reward and threatens punishment. It narrates earlier communities so that later people may take warning. These practices would be pointless, the opponents maintain, without human choice and capacity. The author refers back to the already stated distinction between **having power and acquisition** and being an **independent creator**.

**Third**, Scripture itself employs for human action verbs conventionally expressing production: *ʿamila* ('worked/did'), *faʿala* ('did'), *ṣanaʿa* ('made'), *kasaba* ('acquired'), *jaʿala* ('made or assigned'), and even *khalaqa* ('fashioned or created'). Illustrations include 'Whoever does good, it is for his own sake', statements about what people make or earn, divine reward according to deeds, people placing their fingers in their ears, and the description of ʿĪsā fashioning the form of a bird from clay. They also invoke the occurrence of *iḥdāth* (bringing about) and *ibtidāʿ* (originating), as when the Qurʾān speaks of monasticism people innovated. Al-Taftāzānī answers that these expressions can designate **ordinary occasioning and attributable doing**, as when one says 'the emir built the city' although he employed builders. In particular, *kasb* may be literal on the Sunnī doctrine; *khalq* sometimes means proportioning and fashioning, and *jaʿl* can mean causing a new arrangement or designation without independent creation of an external thing. Al-Rāzī's explanation that the effective complex of power and motive belongs to the servant while the complex itself is produced by God also avoids simply calling all the human predications figurative. It does not, however, yield the complete independence required by the Muʿtazilite position.

**Fourth**, verses admonish unbelievers and sinners for rejecting what they could obey or believe: 'What prevented people from believing?', 'How do you disbelieve in God?', 'What prevented you from prostrating?', 'Why do they not believe?', and similar rebukes. If God Himself created their unbelief, knew and willed it, and provided the motives which ensured it, the objector says that Scripture would seem to make their protest rather than their condemnation valid. The Persianate minister al-Ṣāḥib ibn ʿAbbād is quoted with a series of rhetorical contrasts: commanding faith while not willing it, prohibiting disbelief while willing it, creating religious error while reproaching those who err, and the like. The reply distinguishes readily recognized **external barriers of which the admonished person is conscious** from the deeper account of the created determinants governing events. The historical quotations represent polemical assertions within the debate, not the settled meaning of each Qurʾānic verse.

**Fifth**, verses explicitly make a human deed conditional on human willing: 'Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve' (Q 18:29), 'Do what you will' (Q 41:40), and the descriptions of those who will to advance, fall back or choose a way to their Lord. The author grants human willing but invokes **«وما تشاؤون إلا أن يشاء الله»**: human willing itself depends upon divine willing.

Al-Rāzī's position is then summarized: scriptural expressions can be marshalled on both sides. He gives much weight to rational proof, above all the requirement of a **determining motive** and the argument from **eternal foreknowledge**. A witty opponent reportedly called these the two great enemies of the Muʿtazilite position. An argument from divine willing is weaker as a common premise in a dispute with those who deny that God's willing a human to act always entails his doing so. The story of ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd and a Magian interlocutor displays the polemical paradox: if God desires the interlocutor's conversion but demons frustrate Him, the interlocutor says that he would rather follow the stronger partner.

## The concluding qualification: neither naked compulsion nor complete delegation

The author reports al-Rāzī's observation that this problem is unusually persistent because powerful intuitive considerations pull in both directions. The determination argument says that the obtaining of one alternative over another needs a decisive ground not independently supplied by the servant. The moral-practice argument says that if the servant lacks effective choice, praise, blame, command and prohibition appear unintelligible. One side notes how little an agent knows of the full details of his action; the other that the deed regularly conforms to his intention. One appeals to the imperfection of servants and the dignity of divine creative power, the other to the divine transcendence from human folly and wickedness. Even stories and games are used as emblems of differing intuitions.

The endorsed mediating formula is **«لا جبر ولا تفويض ولكن أمر بين أمرين»**—'Neither sheer compulsion nor complete delegation, but a matter between the two.' The **proximate principles** of human voluntary acts lie in the person's power and willing; their **remoter principles** depend upon what the person does not control. The author also retains the severe determinist image that a person can be constrained in the guise of a chooser, as the peg is driven into the wall by the mallet or the pen moves in the writer's hand. The coexistence of these expressions is part of the source, not to be smoothed into a modern account of libertarian agency.

## *Qaḍāʾ* and *qadar*

Across religious communities it is widely said that things come to pass through divine decree and determination. On the doctrine defended here this includes the deeds of servants, either because God produces the acts themselves or because He creates the power and determining motive by which they occur. One usage of *qaḍāʾ* and *qadar* is **bringing into existence and proportioning**, illustrated by God's determining the seven heavens and apportioning the sustenance of the earth. Other usages are **commanding or obligating**, in such phrases as the divine decree that only God be worshipped; and **making known and announcing**, as in the prophecy concerning the Children of Israel or Lot's wife. The different senses matter: an opponent cannot without argument move from decree as **command** to decree as the **creative production of every event**, or reverse the inference.

The **philosophers' account** is also reported. The total forms of particulars and universals are present in the intelligible world through the Necessary First's production. Because matter cannot receive all particular forms at once, divine bounty provides a temporal order through which these forms pass from potency into actuality. **Decree** can thus signify their comprehensive coexistence in the intelligible order, whereas **determination** signifies their successive particular realization in external matter. The scriptural expression that the treasures of all things are with God and that each is sent down in due measure is invoked analogically. On this philosophical view evil enters divine providence only incidentally. Things may be unalloyed goods, as in their account of separate intellects and celestial spheres, or predominantly good, as in the sublunary world. Rain promotes fertility but also destroys some houses; avoiding the lesser harm by giving up the greater good would itself be a greater loss. The author reports this explanatory doctrine without endorsing all its cosmological presuppositions.

The concluding section begins with the dispute about applying the name **Qadarites** to the two opposing theories of divine decree. The author claims that traditions criticizing the Qadarites refer to those who deny the comprehensive determination of good and evil by God; his opponents argue that the title more naturally belongs to people who affirm rather than deny decree. The subsequent transmitted anecdotes and the question of **generated effects** (*tawallud*) are treated in the next unit.

title: Naming the Qadarites; the reports ascribed to ʿAlī; and generated actions (*tawallud*)
en:
The controversy over *al-Qadariyya* continues. The author invokes the report in which, on Resurrection Day, the Qadarites are summoned as God's adversaries, comparing the Magians' allocation of good and evil to two distinct principles with a person's claim to be the independent determiner of some events. On this argument, someone who attributes part of production to himself stands closer to the disputed appellation than one who refers the whole of decree to his Lord. The opponents reply by citing reports that apparently condemn an excuse based on predestination: people were said to defend forbidden sexual acts as 'God's decree upon us', and an exchange with ʿAlī after Ṣiffīn is recounted in which he denies that decree requires unavoidable compulsion. Were it so, the report says, recompense, threats, promises, command, prohibition, praise and blame would cease to have their proper force; divine command is given with an alternative and prohibition as a warning, not in a universe of absolutely coerced worshippers and sinners.

The author argues that these reports condemn the **inference from decree to moral licence and the abolition of responsibility**, not the proposition that events are encompassed by divine creation and determination. He also contests the attribution and deployment of certain anecdotes by Muʿtazilite polemicists. A sermon ascribed to ʿAlī is cited affirming belief in decree, its good and its evil; another saying describes the futility of escaping a divinely determined outcome. A disputant who says he possesses good, evil, obedience and disobedience is asked whether he possesses them **with God** (suggesting a competing producer) or **without God** (suggesting autonomous divinity). In another anecdote, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq questions a Qadarite's recitation of **«إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين»**—'You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help'—if the servant independently produces the action after all requisite capacities and opportunities are supplied. These are **historical and polemical report claims**, not verified chains of transmission; an edition must check them individually.

## Appendix: actions generated from other actions

The Muʿtazila allow that an act produced directly by a servant may generate a further act, either in the locus of created power or elsewhere. This is their doctrine of **tawallud**, the generation of secondary effects. It raises disputes about whether a generated act can instead be produced directly without an intermediary cause; whether divine acts contain any comparable generation or all are direct; and whether death resulting from a wound is a humanly generated act. Since the author has maintained that possibilities depend upon God's production, he rejects *tawallud* as an account of an **independent created efficient agency**. The Muʿtazila cite the occurrence of an effect according to human intention and motive, and the propriety of praise, blame, command and prohibition, to claim the generated effects as human acts. In fact, artistic work, written words, pushing, pulling, killing and fighting commonly display the human intention more clearly than the immediately produced bodily motions, and moral attribution attaches most readily to the effect. The author's reply repeats the distinction between **attributable acquisition** and **independent creation**.

Reported Muʿtazilite positions diverge. Al-Naẓẓām restricts a servant's act to what arises **in the locus of his power**, assigning later effects to the natures of their loci. Muʿammar assigns the servant only **will**, and subsequent effects to the natures of the things affected; a further position restricts the servant's own act to **thinking**. Other objections say that if generated effects were genuinely ours they would match our intentions invariably, whereas artisans often undo defective work, and that the servant should retain the power to refrain after setting the cause in motion. A released arrow, however, continues its course after release. Replies invoke **interfering conditions**, errors in preparing the causal setup and the completion of the effective conditions: failure to obtain the desired quality, and inability to stop a process after its sufficient antecedent has been supplied, do not alone make that process unrelated to the earlier agent.

The Sunnī authors offer four arguments. **First**, if two people pull or push an object in incompatible directions, an ensuing motion must be due to both, one, or neither; each alternative seems to generate a problem of independent causes or unexplained preference. Al-Taftāzānī questions whether the argument assumes each person could independently have produced **precisely this resultant motion**, rather than merely some motion. **Second**, if the remote effect were within the servant's independent power, why should the servant not produce it directly without the intermediary, as divine power is said to be able to do? **Third**, the Muʿtazila themselves treat a sufficient immediate cause, when no impediment exists, as necessitating its result; this seems to make the initial act independently productive of the result with no further present influence of created power. **Fourth**, a generated effect may occur long after the putative agent's power has disappeared: a person shoots an arrow, then dies, while the arrow wounds another at a later date, with pain or death following still later. The Muʿtazilite reply distinguishes the conditions of eternal and created powers and says that the servant's power operated in the **earlier cause that necessitated the generated result**. Finally, the author recalls the Sunnī position that created power does not independently extend to what occurs **outside its own locus**, although God may create associated events. He cautions that the four arguments, even if sound, must be inspected to see whether they prove **that full thesis** or merely refute some of the opponent's claims.

**End of the first investigation on human acts.** The next investigation concerns the universality of the divine will.

It raises disputes about whether a generated act can instead be produced directly without an intermediary cause; whether divine acts contain any comparable generation or all are direct; and whether death resulting from a wound is a humanly generated act. Since the author has maintained that possibilities depend upon God's production, he rejects tawallud as an account of an independent created efficient agency. The Muʿtazila cite the occurrence of an effect according to human intention and motive, and the propriety of praise, blame, command and prohibition, to claim the generated effects as human acts. In fact, artistic work, written words, pushing, pulling, killing and fighting commonly display the human intention more clearly than the immediately produced bodily motions, and moral attribution attaches most readily to the effect. The author's reply repeats the distinction between attributable acquisition and independent creation.

Reported Muʿtazilite positions diverge. Al-Naẓẓām restricts a servant's act to what arises in the locus of his power, assigning later effects to the natures of their loci. Muʿammar assigns the servant only will, and subsequent effects to the natures of the things affected; a further position restricts the servant's own act to thinking. Other objections say that if generated effects were genuinely ours they would match our intentions invariably, whereas artisans often undo defective work, and that the servant should retain the power to refrain after setting the cause in motion. A released arrow, however, continues its course after release. Replies invoke interfering conditions, errors in preparing the causal setup and the completion of the effective conditions: failure to obtain the desired quality, and inability to stop a process after its sufficient antecedent has been supplied, do not alone make that process unrelated to the earlier agent.

The Sunnī authors offer four arguments. First, if two people pull or push an object in incompatible directions, an ensuing motion must be due to both, one, or neither; each alternative seems to generate a problem of independent causes or unexplained preference. Third, the Muʿtazila themselves treat a sufficient immediate cause, when no impediment exists, as necessitating its result; this seems to make the initial act independently productive of the result with no further present influence of created power. Fourth, a generated effect may occur long after the putative agent's power has disappeared: a person shoots an arrow, then dies, while the arrow wounds another at a later date, with pain or death following still later. The Muʿtazilite reply distinguishes the conditions of eternal and created powers and says that the servant's power operated in the earlier cause that necessitated the generated result. Finally, the author recalls the Sunnī position that created power does not independently extend to what occurs outside its own locus, although God may create associated events. He cautions that the four arguments, even if sound, must be inspected to see whether they prove that full thesis or merely refute some of the opponent's claims.

End of the first investigation on human acts. The next investigation concerns the universality of the divine will.

title: The second investigation: the scope of divine will
en:
The people of truth maintain that **God's will pertains to every event that actually occurs** and does not pertain to an event that does not occur. This is associated with the transmitted maxim, 'What God wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur.' Some scholars nevertheless disapprove of specifying the distasteful instances aloud—saying, for example, 'God wills unbelief or oppression'—although they affirm in general that God creates all things; similarly, one may avoid ostentatiously naming filthy or despised objects when speaking of His creation. The Muʿtazila make a different substantive claim: God wills the unbeliever's faith, though it does not occur, and does not will the unbelief that does occur. He wills obedience from the transgressor rather than the transgression. On their account, much of what happens among servants is contrary to the divine will.

The author remarks polemically that a master whose wishes were so commonly frustrated would scarcely govern an ordinary village. A well-known anecdote contrasts al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār's invocation of God's transcendence above shameful deeds with al-Ustādh Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī's response: glory to the One in whose dominion only what He wills occurs. The attempted defence—that God wants a willing, uncoerced conversion, so a person's rejection does not diminish His power, just as a king may want guests freely to enter his palace but not coerce them—is rejected on the ground that the specified willing **still does not come to pass** when the guests stay out. For the main thesis, the author argues that God produces actual events by His power without coercion and so wills them: will is precisely the attribute specifying one side rather than the other. Likewise, He knows that what will not occur will not occur; a will directed to bringing it about would be incompatible with the function of this specifying attribute.

An objection notes that the contrary of what is eternally known is intrinsically within power. An intrinsically possible and beneficial action could, it says, be willed, even though the agent knows it will not in fact occur. A prophet might tell a person truly that someone will inevitably kill him; he can know that the killing will occur and nevertheless wish to live rather than be killed. The reply distinguishes **wishing or longing** (*tamannī*) from **efficacious specifying willing** (*irāda*): the latter determines the relevant occurrence. The author adduces many verses in which guidance, refusal to believe, opened or constricted breasts, purification, punishment and the call to the abode of peace are explicitly linked to what God wills (for example, Q 6:111 and 6:125; Q 11:34; Q 6:35 and 6:149; Q 5:41; Q 9:55; Q 28:56; Q 10:25). Their interpretation is disputed. The author judges Muʿtazilite efforts to restrict 'God willing to guide everyone' to a kind of **compulsory guidance** strained and records three rival accounts. Al-ʿAllāf describes it as creating faith and guidance in persons without any choice. Al-Jubbāʾī describes it as producing necessary recognition of the truth of faith by demonstrative evidence. Abū Hāshim, his son, describes it as causing the unbeliever to know that refusal will lead to severe torment. The replies are respectively that the first seems incompatible with the opponent's own strict account of human agency, the second is not yet an act of faith and does not overcome verses saying evidence may remain ineffective, and the third describes knowledge that many rejecters already possess. Q 32:13, in which God could have given every soul its guidance but speaks of filling Hell, is offered against all three restrictions.

The Muʿtazila make **eight arguments** for God's non-willing of evil, as reported here.

**(1)** Willing a morally ugly act is itself ugly, whereas God is above ugliness. The reply denies that divine willing has that moral defect and allows that the wisdom of the event may be hidden. **(2)** Punishing for what He wills would be oppression. The reply appeals to God's unrestricted dominion, though the metaphysical assumptions of this reply are precisely part of the dispute. **(3)** Commanding what one does not will and forbidding what one does will would be folly. Al-Taftāzānī replies that an imperative need not aim simply at producing its literal object: a master can order a servant to test obedience or expose disobedience; a person under duress may be forced to issue a command to surrender property. Thus the will behind an *act of commanding* should not without further argument be identified with an absolute will that the commanded action occur. That people normally infer a sovereign's preference from his command relies on contextual signs, not on the bare semantic identity of command and will.

**(4)** If disbelief were willed by God it would be obedience, since obedience means achieving the one obeyed's will. The reply distinguishes obedience as **conformity to command**, which does not automatically coincide with an unexpressed creative will. **(5)** If unbelief is divinely willed, it belongs to divine decree, with which believers must be pleased; but believers must not be pleased with unbelief. The answer distinguishes God's *decreeing* from the *thing decreed* (*qaḍāʾ* from *maqḍī*). Being satisfied with divine wisdom and judgement does not amount to moral approval of an unbeliever's act. A proposed refinement—approving unbelief solely in respect of its being within divine decree while disapproving it in itself—is mentioned but not unreservedly accepted: **'there is a difficulty in this'**.

**(6)** Qurʾānic verses deny that God wishes oppression for His servants, commands indecency, approves unbelief or loves corruption, and rebuke idolaters who invoke divine willing to excuse their idolatry (including Q 3:108; 40:31; 7:28; 39:7; 2:205; 51:56; 6:148). The author interprets the denial of divine oppression as excluding any oppression **by God Himself**. He distinguishes God's creating an act from His approving, loving or commanding the act, because love and approval involve commendation or acceptance. Thus He may bring about the unbeliever's disbelief while prohibiting it and holding its agent responsible. The rebuke of the idolaters is interpreted as directed at their **mockery and attempt to excuse wrongdoing**, not their recognition of divine providence. He notes the wording 'they denied' (*kadhdhaba*) and argues that the same scriptural passage stresses that God could have guided all if He had willed. These are proposed exegetical replies, not self-evident grammatical resolutions of the contest.

**(7)** 'I created jinn and humankind only to worship Me' (Q 51:56) seems to make worship the universal divine intention. The reply first disputes its unrestricted reference, considering those dying in infancy, without capacity, or in unbelief. More importantly, the surrounding statement that God needs neither sustenance nor food is taken as indicating **the creatures' dependence upon Him**, rather than an unconditionally realized purpose to obtain worship from every individual. 'That they should be My servants' and a sense of creaturely subjection are noted as possible interpretations; verses concerning those created for Hell and those allowed to increase in wrongdoing are mentioned as countervailing expressions. The author objects to freely treating every purposive particle as the 'lām of eventual consequence': such an analysis, he argues, is ordinarily appropriate when an agent aims at one end through ignorance and in fact obtains the opposite, which cannot simply be attributed to an omniscient agent.

**(8)** Scriptural characterization of prohibited acts as *disliked* (*makrūh*) appears to make them objects of divine dislike, which would exclude their being willed. The reply distinguishes moral disapproval, the humanly recognized ugliness of such acts, and the technical divine will that produces an event. It cautions, however, that rewriting *makrūh* merely as 'forbidden' in a context already listing prohibitions adds little to the sentence. The treatment thus closes on the recurring distinction between **creative willing, command, love, approval and prohibition**.

title: Third investigation: rational and scriptural evaluation (*ḥusn* and *qubḥ*)
en:
## The precise matter in dispute

The controversy over good and evil (*ḥusn*, *qubḥ*) is included under divine acts, although divine acts do not receive the particular predicates of goodness and badness under discussion, namely **being commanded or prohibited by revealed law**. It belongs here because the acts in question are among the effects of divine creation, and because the opponents' account reaches the acts of God through what it declares obligatory or impermissible for Him. It is commonly said that goodness and badness are, according to our school, **established by revelation** (*sharʿiyyān*) and, according to the Muʿtazila, **known by reason** (*ʿaqliyyān*). This concise formula needs careful definition.

The disagreement is **not** whether intellect recognizes perfection and imperfection—knowledge and ignorance are obvious instances—or what accords with or frustrates purposes, as in conventional assessments of justice and oppression. Reason can recognize such evaluations even without receiving a revelation. The contested sense is **whether an action merits praise or blame in God's judgement, and reward or punishment in the hereafter**. According to our school, revelation itself determines this normative status. An act is good because it is commanded, or bad because it is prohibited; no intrinsic property, different aspect or relational feature of the act independently makes it worthy of that revealed judgement. An act that God had forbidden would, were He to command it instead, bear the relevant status of goodness, and conversely. The Muʿtazila maintain that an act has a good-making or bad-making ground **already knowable by reason**, either immediately (profitable truthfulness and harmful lying), through investigation (beneficial lying and harmful truthfulness), or by the report of revelation (fasting at appropriate times and fasting on a festival day). In the last case the difference remains: for us the command or prohibition **constitutes** the relevant religious quality; for them it **discloses a quality** belonging to the act in itself or in its circumstances. The author refers the various definitions across the schools to his juridical works, including his commentary on *al-Tanqīḥ* and his discussions of the *Mukhtaṣar al-uṣūl*.

## Seven arguments given for the revelation-dependent account

**First.** If goodness and badness had the disputed rational status independently of revelation, someone neglecting a duty or committing a prohibition could deserve divine punishment before any prophet had been sent. In the opponents' own account God must punish an unrepentant person who has incurred that desert. Yet the Qurʾān says, **«وما كنا معذبين حتى نبعث رسولا»** (Q 17:15): 'We were not to punish until We had sent a messenger.' This is offered against the opponents' stronger theory of punishment.

**Second.** On the premises concerning human motivation, acts would be either necessary or fortuitous, and neither is rationally praiseworthy or blameworthy in the sense required. If the servant cannot refrain, the action is compelled. If the servant can refrain and no further preponderating determinant is required, one possibility occurs without sufficient determination. If a determinant is required and is produced by the servant, the question recurs; if not, then either the determinant necessitates the act and human independence fails, or it does not, and the same unexplained selection returns. The opponent says that will is itself a power of specification, and necessity following voluntary choice does not destroy choice or accountability. Al-Taftāzānī replies with the earlier conclusion that decisive motivation arises from something not independently supplied by the servant. He rejects the objection that the reasoning contradicts experience and the parallel objection from divine action by appealing to the earlier qualifications.

**Third.** If a lie's badness belonged to its essence and could never change, lying to rescue a prophet from an otherwise unavoidable death would remain prohibited. Yet saving the prophet is obligatory, and on the stipulated facts lying is the only possible means to do so. The opponent distinguishes the continued badness of the lie from the greater ugliness of allowing the prophet to die; one must choose the lesser evil. Perhaps even a verbal equivocation (*taʿrīḍ*) would avoid a direct lie. Al-Taftāzānī answers that when the lie is genuinely the sole route to an obligatory rescue, it itself becomes obligatory, and hence good in the relevant normative sense. Similar considerations apply to killing or beating when legally prescribed rather than oppressive.

**Fourth.** The claim that truthfulness and falsehood have invariably opposed intrinsic moral statuses is pressed with a **self-referential semantic puzzle**. Someone declares, 'Tomorrow I shall lie.' If the assertion is true, it implies that a lie will occur; if false, then its falsity might ensure that the forecast is not fulfilled. Various formulations attempt to make truth and falsehood, or goodness and badness, follow from one another. A sharper case makes a proposition assert its own falsehood: **'This very statement that I am now uttering is not true.'** If true, it is false; if false, it is true. A two-day variant has one utterance say that the following day's speech is false and the next day's speech affirm that the earlier utterance was true. Al-Taftāzānī calls it a puzzle that has bewildered capable minds and says that, despite searching earlier answers, he has not found a satisfactory solution. He tentatively distinguishes truth or falsity **as a condition of a judgement** from the predicate 'true' or 'false' **within a judgement**. The two might concern different logical referents. Yet, after considering the apparent rescue, his explicit conclusion is that **the right course is to forgo a definitive answer and acknowledge inability to solve the difficulty**. An edition must preserve this admission instead of retroactively presenting a modern resolution as his settled view.

**Fifth.** If an action's goodness were an additional intrinsically existent property, the property would have to inhere in the action, itself an accident. This would yield an accident in an accident, rejected by the opponents' ontology. The premise that goodness is distinct from the act is supported by the fact that one can conceive the act without conceiving its good or bad status. The opponent disputes the inference from the negation of a predicate to the claim that its opposite is a positive entity: 'non-possible' may cover both the impossible and the necessary. The same reasoning would allegedly make possibility an accident in an accident. The Sunnī reply treats **revealed goodness** as the relation of an eternal divine command to the action, not as a new inhering accidental property of the action, and refers again to the juridical analysis.

**Sixth.** If the normative status of an act were determined independently by its nature or qualifying aspects, God could not freely legislate contrary to that status. This appears to curtail divine choice. The opponent says that God freely wills what accords with His wisdom; a wisdom-based inability to produce ugliness is not an imposed external necessitation. Nor does the Sunnī appeal to eternal divine judgement obviously express a new free choice when the judgement is eternally fixed. The author acknowledges that some versions of the argument are best interpreted as **dialectical challenges** about the relation between eternal judgement and its objects.

**Seventh.** If an act's intrinsic goodness attracts the will and its badness repels it, those properties must somehow precede the act in order to explain the motive. But an actually existing property cannot inhere in a merely future or nonexistent action. The opponent says the relevant determining motive is the agent's **knowledge that the act would be good or bad upon its occurrence**, not an already inhering external accident of goodness in the nonexistent act.

## Six principal arguments of the rationalist opponents

**First and most central.** The goodness of justice and beneficence and the badness of oppression and ingratitude are acknowledged by reasonable people of widely differing beliefs, customs and aims, including those who do not profess prophetic revelation. Some even object to killing animals out of ethical concern. This apparent universal agreement would be inexplicable unless good and bad belonged to the acts and were rationally accessible. The reply distinguishes what they have actually agreed upon: harmony or disharmony with human interests, the shared demands of social life, and praise or blame in the customs of rational people. Such agreement does not establish the specifically contested **desert of divine reward and punishment**. A person without belief in revelation or an afterlife may not even affirm the relevant divine judgement. The opponent's attempted analogy from human praise and blame to divine judgement is therefore not self-validating.

**Second.** Someone equally served by truth and a lie, with no information about revealed laws, would naturally prefer truth; even someone who expects no personal gain will often rescue a stranger from imminent death. The opponent claims that rationally perceived goodness explains this preference. The answer invokes deeply ingrained human interests in a reliable social world and naturally shared sympathy, including a person's ability to imagine the other's danger as his own. The stipulated equality usually concerns the present agent's immediate gain, not **every circumstance and human good**; if absolutely every motive were genuinely equal, the alleged invariable preference would itself require proof. What is observed cannot simply be translated into knowledge of the divine judgement at issue.

**Third.** If reason cannot know that lying is bad and that divine deceit or a morally perverse command is excluded, revelation cannot establish moral obligation without vicious circularity. One first needs reason to judge divine reports true and divine commands wise before trusting a revelation that supposedly teaches those facts. The response refuses the premise that **command is merely evidence of a separate antecedent moral quality**: on the defended account the normative predicate 'obligatory' means precisely that a divine command of obligation relates to the act, and the prohibition analogous to it. Al-Juwaynī warns that saying 'goodness is known only by the law' can misleadingly suggest a quality distinct from the law and subsequently discovered; rather, the revealed commendation itself constitutes this religious sense of goodness. The impossibility of divine lying is treated separately in the discussion of divine speech and truthfulness, where the author claims it can be defended without this circle.

**Fourth.** If it were not intrinsically repugnant for God to display a miracle at the hands of a false claimant, miracles could no longer establish prophetic truth. The reply distinguishes **rational possibility in abstraction** from our firm certainty that the scenario does not occur, an assurance associated with customary and established knowledge. This controversial reply is not to be presented as accepted by both parties.

**Fifth.** An intellect that apprehends God's reality and perfections must recognize the ugliness of associating partners with Him or attributing a spouse, child or deficiency to Him even before any prophetic teaching. The reply says that long-established revealed teachings and deeply familiar patterns of moral assessment can become so second nature that one mistakes their origin for bare immediate rational intuition.

**Sixth.** If the first obligation—reasoning about God and acknowledging an authenticated prophet—were not rationally ascertainable, prophetic instruction would be unable to begin without presupposing itself; this is the familiar 'silencing the prophets' argument already addressed earlier in the book.

## The qualified Ḥanafī or Sunnī mediating position

Because the last two arguments are powerful, some Sunnī scholars, especially among the **Ḥanafīs**, allow that reason can recognize the goodness or badness of **certain matters**: the first obligation, the obligation to accept a truthful prophet and not reject him, and the impermissibility for someone who knows God and His perfections to attribute absurd or degrading deficiencies to Him. The author insists that such a view should not be assimilated wholesale to the Muʿtazilite account. It does not imply **that God is under obligations** determined by an independent rational measure, or that the human being independently creates his actions. God remains the source of the binding judgement and of the created acts, whereas reason is **an instrument for knowing some judgements**. Some cognitive judgements occur without the agent's acquired investigation; others arise with acquisition through sound inquiry. This distinguishes the epistemic role of reason from autonomous legislative authority and preserves the nuance of the reported Ḥanafī position.
